items.title: Half of UK small business websites are faceless
items.excerpt: We checked 1,381 UK small business websites. 751 had no video and named nobody. Here's what we found, sector by sector, and the cheap fixes that work.
items.coverAlt: A laptop on an independent shop counter showing a website whose team photos are grey placeholder silhouettes
items.body:
More than half of the UK small business websites we checked are faceless. 751 of 1,381 sites (54.4%) had no video on the homepage or about page and didn't name a single person behind the business. Seven in ten had no video at all, and three in four didn't put a name to anyone.

We make documentary-style brand films, so I'll be honest: I went in expecting a gap. I didn't expect it to be this wide. Here's what we did, what came out, and what I'd do about it this month if it were my website.

What did we actually check?

On 4 October 2026 we ran an automated check on 1,381 UK small business websites, drawn from two separate places.

783 came from our own prospecting and directory lists, with chains, plcs, charities and non-UK sites taken out. That list leans towards trades, EV charging and building services, because that's who we used to work with. So we didn't want to lean on it alone.

The other 598 came from OpenStreetMap, the free, volunteer-built map. We pulled every business with a website listed across 24 UK cities, covering every nation and English region: independent shops, cafes, restaurants and pubs, food and drink makers, hair and beauty, creative studios, dentists, vets, clinics, gyms, accountants, solicitors and architects. Nobody picked those businesses off a sales list, which makes it the fairer test. We removed brands, chains, charities and public bodies, drew a random sample with quotas by business type, and checked it again by hand.

For each site we looked at the homepage plus one linked about or team page, and recorded a handful of things. Is there any video? Is a real person named? Does the business lean on reviews? Which social platforms does it link to? Same code and the same rules for both sources, so the numbers sit side by side.

The OpenStreetMap sample, the one with no sales bias, came out slightly worse on both counts. 437 of 598 (73.1%) had no video, against 544 of 783 (69.5%) from our lists. 475 of 598 (79.4%) named nobody, against 569 of 783 (72.7%).

How many small business websites have no video?

981 of 1,381 (71.0%). Take trades, EV and building services out and it barely moves: 631 of 905 (69.7%).

No sector gets off lightly. Health, care and fitness did best, and still 108 of 180 (60.0%) had no video. Building services came bottom at 108 of 141 (76.6%), with EV charging and energy close behind at 98 of 130 (75.4%). Among independent shops in the OpenStreetMap sample it was 99 of 122 (81.1%), though that's a small group, so treat it as colour rather than a headline.

What kind of video do the rest have?

Mostly the silent kind. Of the 400 sites with any video, 288 (72.0%) only had self-hosted video, which is usually a muted loop playing behind the headline. Only 112 of 1,381 (8.1%) embedded a playable video, the kind you press play on and hear someone talk.

I get why the loops are there. Site builders make them easy and they make a homepage feel like it's moving. But nobody says anything. A visitor gets a mood and no information, and certainly no sense of who they'd be dealing with.

A slow-motion pour of a flat white has never once answered the question "who am I actually dealing with?"

How many businesses name the people behind them?

Very few. 1,044 of 1,381 (75.6%) didn't name a single person on the pages we checked. Having an about page didn't fix it either. Of the 765 sites with a linked about or team page, 458 (59.9%) still named nobody. An about page with nobody on it is a strange thing to publish, and it's the norm.

Professional services were the most likely to name someone, at 80 of 159 (50.3%), followed by estate and letting agents at 44 of 104 (42.3%). Then it drops off a cliff. Trades named someone on 40 of 205 sites (19.5%), EV charging and energy on 22 of 130 (16.9%), independent retail and makers on 37 of 249 (14.9%), and hospitality, food and drink on 13 of 180 (7.2%). In the OpenStreetMap sample, cafes, restaurants and pubs named a person on 4 of 104 sites (3.8%).

So how many are faceless?

Put the two together, no video and no named person, and you get 751 of 1,381 (54.4%). In the OpenStreetMap sample on its own it's 351 of 598 (58.7%).

More than half of the small business websites we checked had no video and didn't name a single person.

By sector, hospitality, food and drink was the most faceless at 120 of 180 (66.7%), then independent retail and makers at 163 of 249 (65.5%) and EV charging and energy at 83 of 130 (63.8%). Professional services were the least, at 54 of 159 (34.0%), which is still one in three.

Where are businesses putting their trust instead?

Mostly in reviews. 677 of 1,381 (49.0%) showed testimonials, a review widget or a review count, and 467 of those 677 (69.0%) had no video. So on a lot of sites, strangers are doing all the talking while the owner stays out of shot. Google was the most common widget (122 sites), then Trustpilot (57) and Checkatrade (28).

The social links tell a similar story. 195 of 1,381 (14.1%) linked to a YouTube channel, and 99 of those 195 (50.8%) showed no video on the pages we checked. Half the businesses with a YouTube channel are sending visitors off-site to find the video instead of putting it in front of them. TikTok turned up on 100 of 1,381 (7.2%), and 370 of 1,381 (26.8%) linked to none of YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn or Facebook.

Why does a faceless website matter?

Because people buy from people. Someone picking a dentist, a builder, an accountant or a cafe for a works lunch is about to trust a stranger with their mouth, their house, their money or their afternoon. The first thing they want to know is who. A site that answers with a logo, a slogan and a stock photo makes them work harder for that answer, and some of them won't bother.

Reviews help, and I'd never tell anyone to take them down. But they're other people's words about you. They can tell a visitor you turned up on time. They can't show how you talk, what you care about, or whether you're someone they'd get on with. That's what a face, a name and a voice do, and it's what a muted background loop can't.

There's an upside in these numbers too. If more than half of the sites a customer compares are faceless, showing yourself is one of the cheapest ways to stand out. You don't need to beat everyone's design. You just need to be the one who turned up.

What can you do about it this month?

Start with the free stuff and work up. Most of this is an afternoon, not a project.

  1. Name the owner. Put a full name and a role on the homepage and the about page. "Run by" plus a name costs nothing and changes how the whole site reads.
  2. Add one real photo. You, at work, in your actual place of work. A phone by a window in daylight is plenty. Swap out the stock image of a handshake while you're there.
  3. Record a 60 second phone video. Who you are, what you do, who it's for, and what happens when someone gets in touch. Don't script it word for word, just know your three points. If talking to a lens makes you freeze, this guide to being filmed works just as well for a phone as a crew. Then run it through our free video resizer to get versions for your site, Instagram and TikTok from one file.
  4. Put an actual video on the homepage. One people can press play on and hear. If you've already got a YouTube channel, embed the best one near the top instead of linking out. If there's a silent loop up there now, that's the spot.

When you're ready for something with more weight behind it, our free 44-page playbook, Before the camera comes out, walks through finding the story in your business before anyone films anything. And if you want us to make it with you, have a look at how our films work.

How we did it, and what it can't tell you

The crawler visited each site's homepage and one linked about or team page, with a desktop browser setting, a 10 second timeout, one request at a time, and robots.txt respected. Video meant embedded players, HTML video tags and video files, including site-builder background video. A named person meant a full name next to a role, "founded by" or "run by" plus a name, or a team profile. Reviewers' names didn't count.

A few honest limits. Neither sample is random across every UK small business. Our lists skew towards London, the South East and trades, and OpenStreetMap favours mapped, city-based businesses with shopfronts, drawn with quotas. So these figures describe these 1,381 sites, and the combined totals depend on the sector mix. We only checked two pages per site. Automated detection can miss video that loads by script, and it won't count an owner who only gives a first name. Spot checks suggest the "no video" and "no named person" figures may run a few points high, though in 440 OpenStreetMap "no video" sites we found only 2 or 3 missed videos, and 25 random named-person hits were all real staff. Sites that blocked automated visits (87 from our lists, 54 from OpenStreetMap) are missing, and they may be better resourced.

On London: within the OpenStreetMap sample there's no real difference. 63 of 87 London sites (72.4%) had no video, against 374 of 511 (73.2%) elsewhere. We don't name or describe any business, and the site-level data stays private.

Can journalists get the full data?

Yes. If you're writing about small businesses, marketing or trust online, I'm happy to share the sector tables, the confidence intervals and the full method, and to talk it through. Email our contact page or get in touch through the contact page.

faqs.q: How was the website audit done?
faqs.a: We used an automated crawler on 4 October 2026 to check 1,381 UK small business websites, 783 from our own prospect lists and 598 sampled from OpenStreetMap across 24 UK cities. It looked at each homepage and one linked about or team page, recording video, named people, reviews and social links, with the same rules for both sources.

faqs.q: Is the sample representative of all UK small businesses?
faqs.a: Not strictly, and we say so. Neither source is a random draw of every UK small business. Our lists lean towards trades and the South East, and OpenStreetMap favours city businesses with shopfronts. The figures describe these 1,381 sites, but the two samples point the same way, which is why we're confident the pattern is real.

faqs.q: Can I get the underlying data?
faqs.a: Journalists and researchers can have the sector tables, confidence intervals and full method. Email the contact page at s4digi.com/contact or use the contact page. We don't share which businesses were checked, because the point of the study is the pattern across the sample, not any single website.

faqs.q: What's the quickest fix for a faceless website?
faqs.a: Put the owner's full name and role on the homepage today. It's free and takes minutes. Next, add one real photo of you at work, then record a 60 second phone video saying who you are and who you help, and embed it where visitors can press play and hear you.

items.title: Why a good film still needs a business goal
items.excerpt: Filming on its own rarely moves anything. Why a brand film works harder when the creative is tied to a real business goal, and how to set that goal first.
items.coverAlt: A team round a table talking through a shoot at the Fully Charged show
items.body:
Filming on its own often isn't enough because a film only earns its money when it's attached to something the business is actually trying to do. A launch, a hiring push, a sales process where buyers keep stalling, a campaign that needs something at the centre of it. Decide that job first and the creative usually gets better, because it finally has something to aim at.

When I was younger it was all creative for me. Now the work has to add to a goal. I care about how a film looks as much as I ever did. I've just stopped thinking that's the whole job.

What does creative mixed with performance actually mean?

It's an awkward phrase, so here it is plainly. Creative is the idea and the craft: the story, who's in it, how it's shot and how it's cut. Performance is what happens once it's out: who sees it, what they do next, and whether that moved the business forward.

Most production companies only really own the first half. Most performance marketers only own the second. The films that pull their weight have both in the room from the start. That doesn't mean turning a documentary into an advert with a discount code in the corner. It means knowing, before anyone picks up a camera, who the film is for, where they'll come across it and what you'd like them to do afterwards. That shapes everything from who we interview to how long the cut runs.

Why do so many well made films do nothing?

Because nobody decided what they were for. A business spends real money on a lovely film, it gets a round of compliments on LinkedIn, it goes on the homepage, and six months later nobody can say what it did. The film wasn't bad. It just never had a job.

A film without a job drifts towards the safe middle. It tries to say everything about the company to everyone, so it says very little to anyone in particular. You can often spot one by the running time: ten minutes long because there was ten minutes of nice footage, rather than because the audience needed ten minutes.

A film without a job tries to say everything to everyone, and ends up saying very little to anyone.

How do you tie a film to a business goal?

Start with one sentence: after watching this, the right person will do something. Fill it in with something you could actually notice. Book a survey. Apply for the role. Enter the competition. Stop asking your sales team the same three questions. If you can't finish that sentence yet, you're not ready to film.

Then work backwards. Who is that person, and where are they when they'd watch it? A facilities manager reading a proposal at their desk wants something very different from a homeowner scrolling on a Sunday night. That decides the length, the format, whether it needs subtitles to work on mute, and which cut-downs you'll need on top of the main film.

Our Christmas raffle film for Plug In Stations and Ohme is the plainest example I've got. The goal was entries from people who genuinely needed a charger, rather than a pile of likes from people who wanted something free. So the film was cut for paid social and run as a Facebook ad, with a golden ticket download that gave people a reason to finish the form. It brought in a thousand entries, and two paid installs on top of the two winners.

Does the goal change what you actually film?

All the time. A few of ours show how much.

  • Selling the next event. At Fully Charged, the South show produced the material that promoted the North one. The real deadline was the start of ticket sales, so the turnaround mattered as much as the footage.
  • Earning trust before a quote. The Barry Road film is the homeowner's account of a full renovation, made for the builder to send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. That's why the builder barely appears.
  • Getting shared by one account. On Musk City the brief was shareability rather than reach. One retweet from the right account could have more than tripled the return, so everything was built and bought around that single outcome.

Three goals, three very different films. If we'd shot all of them to a brief of "make us look good", none of them would have done what it needed to.

Does performance thinking make films worse?

It can, if it's done clumsily. Take a good story, cram in a logo every eight seconds, add a voiceover listing features and finish on a hard sell, and people feel it and leave. Done well, most performance thinking happens in the decisions before and after the film, and the story itself is left alone.

Nobody has ever shared a film because the logo was bigger.

One of the best known examples of the two working together is Volvo Trucks' The Epic Split from 2013. Jean-Claude Van Damme does the splits between two reversing lorries. It's a ridiculous, memorable piece of creative, and the whole thing exists to prove one product claim, how precise Volvo's Dynamic Steering is. The idea and the sales point are the same thing, which is why people still remember both.

You don't need Van Damme for that principle to work. In the showroom install we filmed in Poole, the installer runs a live RCD test on camera to prove a safety feature instead of just claiming it. For an audience of electricians, that test is the most persuasive minute in the film, and it's also the most watchable.

What should you measure once the film is out?

Measure the thing you wrote in that one sentence. Views tell you it was seen. They don't tell you whether it worked. If the goal was hiring, count applications and ask candidates whether they watched it. If it was sales, ask your team whether they're sending it before calls and whether those calls got easier. If it ran as an ad, look at the cost per enquiry rather than the cost per view.

Some of that is soft, and you'll have to ask people. That's fine. A film that's earning its keep usually shows up in what your team tells you as much as in a dashboard.

Where should you start?

Before you ask anyone for a quote, write down the goal and the budget. Then the first conversation with a production company starts in the right place, and you'll be able to judge whatever they propose. There's more on that in how to write a video brief, and our free guide Before the camera comes out walks through the planning in full. If you'd rather talk it through, tell us what the film needs to do. If we don't think a film is the right tool for that goal, I'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What's the difference between brand and performance marketing?
faqs.a: Brand marketing builds how people feel about you over time, so they think of you when they're ready to buy. Performance marketing asks for an action now, like a click, a form or a call, and measures it closely. They work best together. A good brand film gives the performance side something worth putting money behind, and the performance side makes sure the right people actually see it.

faqs.q: Can a documentary-style film be used as an advert?
faqs.a: Yes, usually as cut-downs rather than the full film. A four to ten minute documentary rarely works as a cold ad, but a sixty second cut or a vertical piece built around one strong moment can. Plan for it before the shoot so you capture moments that stand alone, and check your licence and music cover paid advertising on every platform you'll use.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see results from a brand film?
faqs.a: It depends on the job you gave it. A film running as an ad or supporting a launch should show something within weeks. A film made for sales conversations or hiring builds more slowly, because it works each time someone watches it before a decision. That's why you decide what you'll measure before it's published, so you're judging it against the right thing.

faqs.q: What if we just want a film that shows who we are?
faqs.a: That's a fair starting point, but push it one step further. Who needs to know who you are, and what do you want them to do once they do? Usually there's a real answer underneath, like winning bigger clients, hiring better people or standing out from competitors who sound the same. Name that and the film gets sharper without losing any of its character.

items.title: How to turn one brand film into a year of content
items.excerpt: How one brand film becomes a year of content: cut-downs, verticals, stills, quotes, behind the scenes and subtitled versions, and why it's planned at the shoot.
items.coverAlt: An engineer at work on a drainage job, from one shoot day that fed months of content
items.body:
You turn one brand film into a year of content by planning for it at the shoot, then cutting the material into versions that each do a different job: the main film, a short cut, vertical cut-downs, stills, quotes, behind the scenes and subtitled versions in every aspect ratio. Spread those across twelve months and one shoot can feed your channels for most of the year.

The mistake is treating the main film as the only output and everything else as an afterthought. Most of what fills the year has to be captured on purpose, on the day.

Can one brand film really fill a year?

If it's planned properly, yes. Posting once a week is fifty two slots. A documentary-style shoot over two or three days gives you a main film, a sixty to ninety second cut, six to ten vertical pieces and a full set of stills. Add quote posts, carousels, behind the scenes and a few reworked versions, and fifty two stops looking ambitious.

The char.gy B Corp film came to eleven finished exports from a single shoot: a long form film, a sixty second cut and a thirty second cut, each in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1, plus audio described versions, with photography from the same day used across their site. The Super Efficient content day produced an eight minute film, a run of vertical shorts, two carousels and three test thumbnails from one job.

Why does repurposing have to be planned at the shoot?

Because you can't cut what you didn't capture. Vertical pieces need framing with room for a 9:16 crop, or their own setups. Stills need someone shooting them alongside the video. Behind the scenes needs someone filming the crew, which nobody does by accident. Natural sound cuts need clean audio of the work itself.

It also helps to agree the list of outputs before the shoot, in writing. A crew that knows it needs eight verticals and a carousel films differently from one that only knows about the main film. They'll grab the extra angle, hold a shot a few seconds longer and ask the follow-up question that becomes a standalone clip.

Interviews matter most. If you want quotes and short clips that stand on their own, the questions have to produce answers that make sense without the question in front of them. That's a technique you plan for, and it's very hard to rescue in the edit.

You can't cut what you didn't capture.

What can you make from one brand film?

The main film

Usually four to ten minutes. It goes on your website, YouTube, in sales conversations and at events. Cut it first, because everything shorter comes out of it.

The short cut

Sixty to ninety seconds for the top of your site and anywhere nobody will give you ten minutes. It has to work as its own piece rather than a trailer for the long one.

Vertical cut-downs

Each one should have a different job. On Super Efficient one was the satisfying moment the drain clears, one was the reveal of what was actually down there, and one was the two engineers talking straight to camera about the trade. Sound was left alone rather than buried under music, because on a job like that the sound is half the appeal.

Stills

Photographs shot across the same days, so the film and the pictures look like the same company. They'll cover your website, LinkedIn, press and proposals for months.

Quotes

The best lines from the interviews become quote posts, carousel slides, captions, website copy and sales deck slides. Use the exact words. Never tidy up what someone actually said, because the slightly rough version is the one people believe.

Behind the scenes

The setup, the lighting, the nervous moment before the first question. People like seeing how things are made, and it puts a human face on your business that a polished film doesn't always show. It's also useful the week before launch, as a teaser that tells people something's coming without giving the film away.

Subtitled and accessible versions

Every cut should have a subtitled version, because a lot of video is watched on mute. Think about audio description too. char.gy serves drivers who are usually left out, so an inaccessible film about inclusion would have been a bad look. The audio described cut was part of the brief from the start.

How do you spread it across twelve months?

A rough shape that works for most businesses:

  • Month one. Launch the main film and short cut. A founder post on LinkedIn, an email to your list, the film on the website.
  • Months two to four. One vertical a week, alternating with stills and quote posts.
  • Months five to eight. Carousels, behind the scenes, and the film working inside a specific push like a hiring round or an event.
  • Months nine to twelve. Rerun the best performers with new captions, and use what you've learned to plan the next shoot.

Mix it in with whatever else you post. A year of nothing but one film would be a lot. A year where that film is the backbone, with everyday posts around it, is just good planning.

The footage you didn't use is still footage you paid for.

Won't people get bored of seeing the same footage?

Far less than you'd think. On most platforms only a slice of your followers see any given post, so something you're sick of has probably reached a small part of your audience. Different cuts also do different jobs. Someone who scrolled past the satisfying clip might stop for the engineer talking about the trade.

Watch the numbers and your own gut. When a clip starts to feel dated, because the people, the premises or the offer have changed, retire it. That's usually the point to book the next shoot.

How do you resize a film for every platform?

Ideally it's done in the edit, with each version reframed by hand so nothing important gets cropped. For a quick resize of an existing clip, our free video resizer will get a file into the right shape. For where each version should go once it's cut, see where to put your brand film once it's made.

If you'd like a film that's planned to feed a year from the first conversation, see how our films work or tell us about the business.

faqs.q: How many short videos can you get from one brand film?
faqs.a: From a two or three day documentary shoot, six to ten vertical pieces is realistic, alongside the main film and a sixty to ninety second cut. You can get more if the shoot is planned for it, with extra setups, more interview questions built to stand alone and coverage of moments that work on their own. The limit is usually planning rather than footage.

faqs.q: Should vertical videos be filmed separately?
faqs.a: For the pieces that matter most, often yes. Cropping a 16:9 frame to 9:16 throws away most of the picture and can cut people in half. Framing wide enough to crop safely works for some shots, but a few dedicated vertical setups on the day give you far better results. Tell your production company before the shoot which verticals you'll want.

faqs.q: Do you need subtitles on social video?
faqs.a: Yes. A lot of social video is watched with the sound off, in public places or late at night, and subtitles are the only way your message lands. They also help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and plenty of people who simply concentrate better with them. Burn them into the picture for social, and supply a caption file for YouTube and your website.

faqs.q: Can you repurpose an old brand film?
faqs.a: Often, yes, as long as it still reflects the business. Go back through the original footage, not just the finished film, because there are usually moments and lines that never made the cut. Check the people, premises and offer haven't changed, and check your licence and music cover the new uses. If too much has moved on, it's time for a new shoot.

items.title: How licensing works for music, footage, photos and fonts
items.excerpt: A plain-English map of licensing for brand content: royalty free vs rights managed, Creative Commons, stock footage, fonts and what to do with a claim letter.
items.coverAlt: In the sound suite with a client for the final mix
items.body:
A licence is permission to use somebody else's work in agreed ways, while they keep the copyright. Nearly everything in a piece of brand content is used under one: the music, the stock shot, the photo on the landing page, even the font in the end title. Most copyright trouble comes from using something just outside a licence's edges, not from anyone setting out to steal. This is general guidance from how licensing works in production. It isn't legal advice, so if there's a live dispute or real money involved, talk to a solicitor.

A ninety second film can easily carry five or six separate licences. Nobody reads them all, which is fine until a letter arrives asking who cleared the thumbnail.

What's the difference between a licence and owning the copyright?

In the UK, copyright is automatic. It lasts a long time. The government's guide to how long copyright lasts puts it at 70 years after the author's death for artistic works like photos, and 70 years from first publication for sound recordings.

The owner can sell the copyright outright, an assignment, or keep it and give you permission, a licence. Library purchases are licences. The same applies to films you commission, which we've covered in who owns the footage when you commission a film.

What do royalty free, rights managed and subscription actually mean?

Royalty free means you pay once and can use the item many times within the licence, without paying per view or per use. It doesn't mean free or unowned, and the licence still has limits.

Rights managed means you pay for one defined use. The price depends on how long, where, in what media and how prominently. Archive footage and premium photography often work this way. Use it somewhere new and you need a new licence.

Subscription libraries let you download what you like while you're paying. The thing to read is what happens when you stop. Some keep you covered for anything published during the subscription. Some don't. We covered this for music in music licensing for brand videos, and it applies to footage and photos too.

What do term, territory, platform and media mean in a licence?

  • Term. How long you can use it. Perpetual, a fixed number of years, or only while a subscription runs.
  • Territory. Where it can be shown. Worldwide is common online, but rights managed licences are often narrower.
  • Platform. Which channels. Website, YouTube, LinkedIn, paid social. Paid adverts are the use most often missing.
  • Media. The type of use. Online, broadcast, print, cinema, events, packaging.

Are Creative Commons images free to use for business?

Sometimes, and only on the licence's conditions. Creative Commons offers six licences, built from four elements:

  • BY means you must credit the creator. The CC BY 4.0 deed asks you to give appropriate credit, link to the licence and say if you made changes.
  • SA, share alike, means adaptations have to be shared under the same terms. Build on SA material and your own content may have to go out under that licence too.
  • NC, non commercial, allows use that isn't primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage. Brand content is about as commercial as content gets.
  • ND, no derivatives, means no adaptations. Read it carefully before you crop, grade or put type over it.

CC BY is the friendliest for business, and even that bites if the credit's missing. The licence also says other rights, like publicity and privacy, may limit what you can do. A Creative Commons photo of a person doesn't come with that person's permission to appear in your advert.

Under the 4.0 licences, if you break the terms and fix it within 30 days of finding out, your rights are reinstated automatically, though the creator can still pursue the original breach. Older versions differ, so note the version number.

Giving someone credit isn't the same as having their permission.

Can you use photos you find on Google?

Usually not. Google Images is a search engine, not a library. The Intellectual Property Office's copyright notice on digital images says images found online can be used when the copyright has expired, when you have permission from the owner for exactly what you want to do, or when the use falls under specific exceptions the law allows. Promotional posts rarely fit the last one.

It also makes two points worth knowing. A photographer's name under the picture doesn't license it, because credit and permission are separate things. And deliberately removing metadata that identifies the owner is unlawful in its own right.

The only image licence that never needs checking is the one where you pressed the shutter yourself.

How do stock footage and photo licences work?

Most libraries sell a standard licence and an extended one. Taking iStock's licence summary as a typical example, the standard licence covers most commercial and business uses, and the extended licence is for things like print runs over 500,000 copies and merchandise made for resale. Every library draws those lines differently, so read yours.

Editorial use only. Some clips and photos are licensed for news and description, not for promotion. They usually lack the releases a commercial use needs.

Model and property releases. A release is the signed consent of a person shown, or the owner of a distinctive building or private property.

Sensitive uses and logos. Showing a model alongside something like a health condition usually needs a note that they're a model, and iStock's terms bar using its content in a trademark or logo.

What about archive and news footage?

Archive footage is usually rights managed, licensed for a specific film, term, territory and media, often priced by how much you use. News footage has an extra layer. A news package can contain music or footage the broadcaster doesn't own, and the archive may only clear its own rights. Ask exactly what they're clearing and what's left to you.

Do you need a licence for fonts?

Yes. A font is software, and its licence covers where the font file is used. Monotype's licensing guide splits it out clearly: desktop licences cover installing fonts for print and static images, webfont licences cover embedding them in a website, app licences cover phones, tablets and software products, and digital ad licences cover HTML5 ads and email, up to a set number of impressions.

The common slip is buying a desktop licence for a brand font and then loading it onto the website. For video, check the licence covers on screen titles and broadcast if that's where you're going, because foundries word that differently. Google Fonts are all open source and can be used commercially, mostly under the SIL Open Font License, which is part of why they're everywhere.

Why do businesses get copyright claim letters, and how should you respond?

Mostly because image tracking is automated now. Rights holders, and firms acting for them, scan websites for their photos and write asking for a fee. The usual culprit is an image added years ago from a search result, an old agency or a lapsed subscription.

If one lands:

  1. Don't ignore it, and don't pay straight away. Work out which image and where.
  2. Check your records. If you hold a licence that covers the use, send it.
  3. Check the claimant. Ask them to show they own or represent the work.
  4. Take the image down while you look. It doesn't erase past use, but it stops the problem growing.
  5. If you were in the wrong, negotiate. The first figure isn't always final.
  6. If it's a real dispute, get help. A solicitor is the first call. The IPO runs a mediation service if both sides agree to use it, and the Intellectual Property Enterprise Court has a small claims track for straightforward claims under £10,000.

How should you keep licence records?

The licence only protects you if you can find it. For every third-party asset, keep:

  • What it is, and the file name you used
  • Where it came from, with the page link and the creator's name
  • The licence type and version, with a saved copy or screenshot of the terms
  • Whose account bought it, and the receipt or licence certificate
  • The date, and when it expires if it does
  • Where it's been used, platform by platform
  • Any releases for people or property
  • Any credit line the licence requires

One folder per project, kept after the subscription ends and handed over if you change agency. It's dull, and it turns a stressful letter into a two line reply.

How does this work on our films?

Every film we make comes with a full licence to use everything indefinitely, on every platform, inside the fixed price. So the music, footage and type are chosen to fit that from the start. The films page shows how one comes together, our free playbook Before the camera comes out covers the planning, and if you've got a project in mind, tell us about it.

faqs.q: Is it okay to use an image if I credit the photographer?
faqs.a: No, not on its own. A credit is a courtesy, and sometimes a condition of a licence, but it isn't permission. Unless the copyright has expired or a legal exception applies, you need the owner's permission for the exact use you have in mind. Creative Commons BY licences are the exception that proves the rule: they give permission in advance, on condition you credit properly.

faqs.q: Do we need to keep licences after a stock subscription ends?
faqs.a: Yes. Some libraries keep you covered for anything published while you were subscribed, and the licence records are your proof of that. If a claim arrives years later, the receipt and saved terms are what settle it. Store them with the project, not in the inbox of whoever happened to download the file.

faqs.q: Can we use clips from a TV programme in our marketing video?
faqs.a: Usually only with a licence from the broadcaster or rights holder. UK law has exceptions for things like criticism, review and quotation, but they're narrow and fact specific, and promotional content rarely fits. A clip can also contain music or footage the broadcaster doesn't own, which needs its own clearance. For anything you're unsure about, take advice before it goes live.

faqs.q: Should the licence be in our name or our agency's?
faqs.a: Ideally yours, or at least clearly transferable to you. If an agency or freelancer buys assets under their own account, ask whether the licence covers your use after the job ends and get a copy of it. Otherwise a lapsed subscription or a parted company can leave you with content you can't prove you're allowed to use.

items.title: How long should a brand film be?
items.excerpt: How long a brand film should be: the main film vs cut-downs, what platform limits actually say, and an honest way to tell when a film is too long.
items.coverAlt: A portrait artist beside her work at her exhibition
items.body:
A main brand film usually works best somewhere between four and ten minutes, which is long enough to tell a real story and short enough to hold a viewer who chose to press play. Alongside it you want a sixty to ninety second version for the top of your website, and a handful of short vertical cuts for the feed. The honest answer to how long a film should be is as long as the story holds, and not a second more.

Length gets argued about more than almost anything else in a film. Usually someone wants it shorter because they've heard nobody watches long videos, and someone else wants every customer, every service and every award in it. Both are reasonable instincts. Neither is a good way to decide.

How long should the main brand film be?

Ours usually run four to ten minutes. That's the range where a documentary-style film has room for the bits that make it work: a person explaining something in their own words, a pause before an answer, the work happening at the speed it really happens.

Where in that range it lands depends on the story. One founder and one clear arc might be done in four minutes. La Fromagerie carries four people's accounts of thirty three years of a business, and that needs more room. The film for Super Efficient is an eight minute film of one drainage job, because a homeowner or facilities manager weighing up who to call wants to see the whole thing done properly.

Who's watching matters as much as the story. Someone deciding whether to trust you with a house, a commercial contract or a large invoice will give you ten minutes, because the decision is worth it to them. Someone scrolling on a train won't, and shouldn't be asked to.

A long film that holds attention beats a short one that doesn't. Length is only a problem when the film runs out of things to say.

Why make shorter cut-downs as well?

Because most places a film ends up won't give you ten minutes. The homepage, a LinkedIn post, an email to a cold prospect, a screen on an exhibition stand. Each of those needs a version built for it, rather than the long one trimmed until it fits.

That's why one shoot should give you a set of films. With ours, that's the main film, a sixty to ninety second cut and six to ten vertical pieces. The char.gy B Corp film went further: a long form film, a sixty second cut and a thirty second cut, each delivered in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1, plus audio described versions, which came to eleven finished exports from one shoot.

The Car Planet customer story shows how different those cuts can be. The YouTube film is the customer talking. One vertical edit follows the install start to finish. The other is ten seconds of the charger on the wall, with no people and no site, which is the cut that can run anywhere.

What are the platform limits on video length?

They change often, so check each platform's help pages before you plan around one. At the time of writing, YouTube says its Shorts can be up to three minutes long, and LinkedIn's help centre lists a maximum of fifteen minutes for video posts. Instagram and TikTok have both stretched their limits in recent years too.

Treat those as ceilings. Just because a platform will take a ten minute upload doesn't mean the people scrolling it want one. Vertical cuts tend to work when they do one thing: one moment, one point, one bit of the process. If you need to turn a 16:9 edit into a vertical or square one, our free video resizer does the basic job in the browser.

Does a shorter video always perform better?

For a first impression, short usually wins. In Wyzowl's 2026 survey, 63% of people said a short video was how they'd most like to learn about a product or service, well ahead of articles, infographics, sales calls and webinars.

But short isn't the only job. The char.gy long form film became the most viewed video on their YouTube channel. A longer film earns its place further down the line, when someone's already interested and wants to know whether they believe you. The short cut gets them curious. The long one helps them decide.

Nobody's ever finished a film and said “that was great, but I wish it had a third montage of the office”.

How do you know if a film is too long?

Watch it as a stranger would. If there's a section you'd skip, cut it. If two people say the same thing, keep the one who says it better. Forget the number of minutes and ask whether every part earns the next one.

That's why we show you a rough cut, while changing it is still cheap. It's the point where length is easiest to get right. Once a film's live, YouTube's audience retention data in Studio will show where viewers drop off, which is worth checking on any longer piece to see whether viewers drift off gradually or leave at one particular moment.

Should you decide the length before the shoot?

Roughly, yes. You don't need an exact running time, but you do need to know which versions you want and where each one will live. That decides what gets filmed. A vertical cut needs shots framed with a vertical crop in mind. A thirty second version needs a line that works on its own. If nobody thinks about that until the edit, the short cuts end up being whatever happened to fit.

It shapes the interviews too. If we know there's a thirty second cut to make, we'll make sure someone sums the story up in a sentence or two, in their own words, instead of hoping a usable line turns up by accident.

The planning side of all this is covered in our free playbook, Before the camera comes out. And if you're weighing up what a film and its cuts would cost, the film budget calculator is a decent place to start before you talk to us.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is a ten minute brand film too long for a website?
faqs.a: Not if it holds attention, but it shouldn't be the only version there. Put a sixty to ninety second cut at the top of the page for people who've just arrived, and make the full film available for those who want more. Visitors who are seriously considering you will often watch the long one through, because the decision matters to them.

faqs.q: How long should a brand video for LinkedIn be?
faqs.a: Short enough to make one point, usually well under two minutes for a post in the feed. LinkedIn's help centre lists fifteen minutes as the maximum, but nobody scrolling the feed is asking for fifteen minutes. A sixty second cut from your main film, captioned for silent viewing, is a sensible default. Share the full film as a link for people who want the whole story.

faqs.q: How many cut-downs should we get from one brand film?
faqs.a: Enough to cover every place you'll actually use it. A common set is the main film, one sixty to ninety second version and six to ten short vertical pieces. Some projects need more, like separate edits for different audiences or square versions for particular channels. Agree the list before the shoot, because it changes what gets filmed.

faqs.q: Should a brand film have a fixed running time in the contract?
faqs.a: A target range is helpful, a fixed number usually isn't. Agreeing four to six minutes, say, keeps everyone's expectations aligned and helps plan the shoot. Locking it to an exact second forces the edit to pad or cut for the sake of a number. The rough cut is the right moment to settle the final length, once you can see what the story needs.

items.title: Where to put your brand film once it's made
items.excerpt: Where to use your brand film once it's made: your website, sales conversations, LinkedIn, email, events, recruitment and paid ads, and which cut goes where.
items.coverAlt: A busy exhibition stand at the NEC, filmed for a year of content
items.body:
Put your brand film wherever people are already deciding about you. That means a short cut near the top of your website and the full film on your about page, in your sales conversations and proposals, on LinkedIn, in your emails, on screen at events, in recruitment, and as cut-downs behind paid ads. Most films only ever make it onto the homepage, which is a small fraction of the work they could be doing.

Why do most brand films end up underused?

Launch day gets all the attention. The film goes up, everyone shares it, and then it sits there. Nobody planned where it would go next, so it doesn't go anywhere.

The fix is to plan distribution before the shoot, not after. Each place a film lives needs a slightly different version: a short cut for the homepage, verticals for the feed, a subtitled version for silent autoplay. If you decide where it's going early, those versions get captured on the day instead of being squeezed out of footage that was never shot for them.

Where should a brand film go on your website?

Three places, usually. A sixty to ninety second cut near the top of the homepage, for people who'll give you a minute and no more. The full film on your about page, where people who want to know who you are have already chosen to look. And relevant clips on service pages, so the proof sits next to the thing it proves.

The char.gy B Corp film runs as the principal video on two pages of their site, About and Local Government, with a toggle between the standard and audio described versions. Same film, two audiences, both served from one shoot.

A few practical things. Host it on YouTube or Vimeo rather than uploading a huge file to your own site. Pick a proper poster frame instead of whatever the first frame happens to be. Add captions. And don't autoplay with sound, unless you enjoy people closing the tab.

How do you use a brand film in sales conversations?

This is where a good film earns the most and gets used the least. Send it before a first call, so the prospect turns up already knowing who you are and how you work. Put it in proposals. Send it afterwards for the people in the buying group who weren't on the call, because there's nearly always someone senior who'll make the decision without ever meeting you.

The Barry Road film was made for exactly that. It's the homeowner's account of a full renovation, an edit the builder can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. A prospective client hears it from a person in their own position rather than from the person being paid.

Send it to the person who'll make the decision without ever meeting you.

Should you post your brand film on LinkedIn?

Yes, but not as one post with a YouTube link. Upload it directly so it plays in the feed instead of asking people to click away, and use the short cut or a vertical piece rather than the full film. Make sure it works on mute with subtitles burned in.

Post it from the founder's or a team member's own profile as well as the company page, because people engage with people. Then keep going. One clip a week for a couple of months will reach far more of your network than a single launch post. When we made the Fusion and NexBlue partnership film, it was cut so both businesses could publish it on their own channels, which doubled where it lived from day one.

How do you put a brand film in an email?

Most email clients won't play video inside the message, so don't try to embed it. Use a still from the film with a play button on it, linked to the page where the film lives. A strong frame of a real person usually beats a logo.

Good places for it: your email signature, the welcome or onboarding email for new clients, a newsletter when it launches, and the follow-up after a meeting. If you have a sequence that goes out to new enquiries, the film belongs in the first or second email.

How can a brand film work at events?

On the stand screen, on a loop, with subtitles, because nobody hears anything on a show floor. At the start of a talk you're giving, so the room knows who you are before you say a word. At your own launches, open days and award nights.

Events also make content of their own. At Fully Charged the film from the South show was used to sell tickets to the North one, so one event fed the next.

Can a brand film help with recruitment?

It's one of the most underrated uses. Good candidates check you out the same way buyers do, and a film showing real people doing the real work tells them more than any job description. Put it on your careers page, link it from job ads, and send it to shortlisted candidates before interview. It also makes a good first thing to watch on someone's first day.

A film that only lives on the homepage is a bit like a suit that only gets worn to the fitting.

Should you put ad money behind your brand film?

Behind the cut-downs, often yes. The full film rarely makes a good cold advert to strangers, but a short version with a strong opening can, and the full film works well shown to people who've already visited your site. The Christmas raffle film we made for Plug In Stations and Ohme ran as a Facebook ad rather than an organic post, which is how it reached a thousand entries.

Before you spend anything, check two things: that your licence covers paid advertising, and that the music licence covers every platform you're going to run it on. Our films come with a full licence on every platform, but that isn't standard everywhere.

If you're still at the planning stage, how to turn one brand film into a year of content covers the versions you'll want to capture. And if you'd like a film built with all of this in mind from the start, tell us where it needs to work.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should I host my brand film on YouTube or Vimeo?
faqs.a: Either works, and plenty of businesses use both. YouTube gives you search visibility and a channel people can find on their own, which suits public films. Vimeo gives you a cleaner player with no suggested videos from other channels, which suits embedding on your site and sending in sales conversations. The main thing is not uploading a huge video file directly to your website, which slows the page down.

faqs.q: Should a brand film autoplay on my homepage?
faqs.a: A muted, looping clip can autoplay as a background if it's short and light. The film itself shouldn't, especially with sound. People arrive expecting to read and scroll, and sudden audio sends many of them straight back out. Let them choose to press play, and make sure the poster frame and a line of text give them a reason to.

faqs.q: How often can I repost my brand film?
faqs.a: More often than you'd think, as long as each post uses a different cut or a different angle. Most of your followers won't see any single post, so resharing over months isn't repetition to them. Space it out, change the clip and the caption each time, and lead with a different moment. Retire anything that starts to feel dated.

faqs.q: Can I use my brand film in a pitch deck or presentation?
faqs.a: Yes, and it often works better than slides about who you are. Embed or link a short cut early in the presentation, or play the full film if you've got the time and the room. Download a local copy beforehand in case the venue's internet fails. Check your licence covers this kind of use, though most full licences do.

items.title: How much does a brand film cost in the UK?
items.excerpt: What a brand film really costs in the UK. Ours start at £15,000 + VAT. Here's where the money goes and what other budgets typically buy you.
items.coverAlt: Deborah Carre and James Ducker laughing at the end of their interview in the workshop
items.body:
A documentary-style brand film in the UK typically costs somewhere between £8,000 and £30,000, depending mostly on how much research goes in, how many shoot days it needs and the size of the crew. Ours start at £15,000 + VAT, and most land between £15,000 and £25,000. A simpler corporate video can be done for a few thousand, and there's nothing wrong with that if it fits the job.

I'd rather put the numbers at the top than make you book a call to find them out. Two companies can quote £3,000 and £30,000 for what sounds like the same brief, and both can be fair. The difference is nearly always in what's included, and most of that is work you can't see on the finished film.

Two companies can quote £3,000 and £30,000 for what sounds like the same brief, and both can be fair.

Where does the money go in a brand film?

Pre-production and story development

This is the part most cheaper quotes leave out, and it's the part that decides whether the film is any good. Before anything's filmed we spend time with the business. Who's in it, what they've been through, what nobody outside the company knows. We come back with the story we think it is, and you tell us whether we're right.

On our films that's inside the fixed figure. It's also why a film takes six to ten weeks from the first conversation. You can't really rush it, and if you try, you end up filming the obvious version.

Shoot days

A shoot day is the biggest single unit of cost in any production, because almost everything else scales with it. Crew, kit hire, travel, insurance. Our films usually take two to three days on a cinema camera with proper sound.

One day can work for a tight brief. For documentary it's usually too little, because the good stuff tends to happen once people have stopped noticing the camera.

Crew

Every extra person on set is another day rate. Add a sound recordist or a second camera for interviews and you multiply that by the shoot days. A bigger crew isn't automatically better, but sound is the thing people notice straight away when it's wrong.

Locations

Filming on your own premises costs nothing to hire, which is one reason documentary can be good value. Hired studios, permits and travel all add up, and real locations have their own cost. When we filmed La Fromagerie, the shops were open and trading, and the cheese rooms were cold, dark and full of customers. No hire fee, but a lot of patience and lighting work.

Edit time

This is usually where the most hours go. An interview-led film gets found in the edit: hours of conversation cut down to a few minutes that hold together and still sound like the person. You see it at rough cut, while changing it is still cheap, and again before it's finished. If a quote allows two days of editing for a six minute documentary, it's a quote for a different kind of film.

Grade and sound mix

Colour grading and the sound mix are separate jobs, and at this level they're done by people who only do that. It's the difference between a film that looks expensive and one that looks like a video.

Music licensing

Production library music is affordable and covers most brand films. A commercial track you'd recognise can run into thousands, and the licence is often limited by term, territory or platform. Whoever quotes you should be able to say exactly what the music licence covers.

Cut-downs

One shoot should give you more than one film. With ours you get the main film, usually four to ten minutes, a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of your site, six to ten vertical pieces cut for the feed, and stills from the same days. Cut-downs are where quotes vary the most, so check whether they're in yours or priced on top.

Why is cheap video cheap?

A cheap video is usually one person, one day and one camera, with an edit turned round in a couple of days and a stock track underneath. For plenty of jobs that's the right call. Event recaps, a quick product demo, a talking head for LinkedIn.

Nobody has ever stood up at a screening and said “the cheap one was worth it.” They just quietly stop using the video.

What drops out at that price is the work you can't see. The research. The second shoot day. Time in the edit to find the story instead of just assembling the shots. A proper grade and mix. It tends to say what every other company in your sector says about itself, and people stop watching at about the same point they would with anyone else's.

I'm not knocking it. I'd just rather you knew what you were buying.

What do different video budgets get you in the UK?

These are rough market ranges from what I see across the UK. They aren't our quotes, and you'll find good people charging above and below every one of them.

  • Under £2,000. Usually a freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some b-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple talking heads.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or an experienced freelance team. One or two shoot days, a scripted or interview-led piece, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, and a full set of cuts. Our films sit in this band.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Should you tell a production company your budget?

Yes. I know it feels like handing over your negotiating position, but I'd always rather know the number early. It tells me what's realistic, and it stops us both spending weeks on an idea you can't afford. If your budget's £6,000, I'd much rather say so on the first call and point you somewhere useful than send you a proposal for £20,000 and never hear back.

The other conversation I want early is what the film is for. Filming on its own rarely moves anything. A well made film with no job to do ends up on the homepage and quietly does nothing. The ones that earn their money are tied to something the business is actually trying to do: a launch, hiring, a sales conversation where buyers keep stalling, a campaign that needs something at the centre of it. That decides who's in it, how long it runs, which cuts you need and where they go. It's also the only honest way to judge whether £15,000 is good value or a waste.

How do we price our films?

Every film we make is scoped around the story and quoted as one fixed figure, agreed in full before anything's booked. Research, shooting, the edit, the grade, the mix and a full licence to use everything indefinitely on every platform are all inside it. You won't get a day rate that keeps growing while you watch.

That’s the sort of thing the figure pays for. Two shoemakers, a workshop and a process most people never see, given the time to be told properly.

Where a film lands between £15,000 and £25,000 mostly comes down to how many shoot days the story needs, how many people and places are in it, and how many cuts you want at the end. You can see what that looks like on our films page.

What if a brand film isn't the right spend?

Sometimes it isn't, and I'll tell you. If what you need is a steady run of posts every month, a film is the wrong spend.

  • Spotlight is a one-off personal brand shoot at £795 + VAT.
  • Momentum is a monthly content partnership from £1,800 + VAT a month.
  • Studio is our bigger monthly partnership, from £2,500 + VAT a month.

What should you ask before you accept a video quote?

  • Is research and story development included, or am I writing the brief myself?
  • How many shoot days, and who's on the crew each day?
  • What's the music licence, and when does it run out?
  • Which cuts come back, and in which formats?
  • How many rounds of changes, and at what stage?

If you've got a business you think there's a story in, tell us about it. If we don't think there's a film there, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you get a brand film made for under £5,000?
faqs.a: Yes, you can get a good video made for under £5,000, but it'll usually be a different kind of film. Expect one or two shoot days, a scripted or interview-led piece and a proper edit. What drops out is the research, the extra shoot days and the time in the edit to find the story. For social content, a talking head or a product demo, that's often the right spend.

faqs.q: Do video production quotes in the UK include VAT?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most UK production companies quote prices excluding VAT, and ours do too, so a film at £15,000 + VAT comes to £18,000 once 20% VAT is added. If your business is VAT registered you can normally reclaim it, so the ex VAT figure is the real cost to you. Check which number every quote shows before you compare them side by side.

faqs.q: Who owns a brand film once you've paid for it?
faqs.a: It depends on the licence in the contract, so read it before you sign. Some companies license a film for a set period, one platform or one territory, and charge again to extend it. Ours come with a full licence to use everything indefinitely on every platform, and that's inside the fixed figure. Music is the bit to check hardest, because commercial tracks often carry their own limits.

faqs.q: How do you know if a brand film is worth the money?
faqs.a: You judge it against the job it's meant to do, and you decide that job before anyone films anything. A film tied to a launch, hiring or a sales conversation where buyers keep stalling has a clear way to earn its keep. A film with no job ends up on the homepage doing very little, whatever it cost. If you can't say what someone should do after watching, sort that out first.

stat.takeaway: Most businesses that invest in video see it pay back in leads and sales, so the budget question is really about what the film needs to do for you.

items.title: How to write a video brief a production company can use
items.excerpt: How to write a video brief that a production company can actually use: the goal, audience, budget, sign-off and constraints, and what to leave out of it.
items.coverAlt: A char.gy team member smiling mid-answer in an interview, the City behind her
items.body:
A video brief a production company can actually use explains the problem rather than the solution. It says what the film is for, who it's for, what you want them to do afterwards, where it'll be seen, what the budget is, when it's needed and who signs it off. One or two pages is plenty. Leave the creative approach to the people you're hiring, and give them everything they need to get it right.

The briefs that cause trouble are rarely too short. They're usually full of the wrong things: shot lists and scripts, with no mention of the goal or the money.

What should a video brief include?

Here's the structure I'd use, in roughly the order a production company will want to read it.

  1. The goal. One sentence on what the film needs to achieve for the business. Win bigger clients, hire engineers, launch a product, sell tickets.
  2. The audience. Who's watching, what they already know about you and what they're sceptical about.
  3. The action. What you'd like them to do after watching, and how you'll know they did it.
  4. The story you suspect is there. The founder's history, a customer whose life changed, a craft that took years to learn. You don't need the answer, just your hunch.
  5. The people. Who's available to be filmed, who's good at talking, and who'd rather not.
  6. Where it'll live. Website, sales, LinkedIn, events, ads. This decides the lengths, formats and aspect ratios.
  7. Budget. A number, or at least a range and a ceiling.
  8. Timings. Fixed dates like a launch or an event, and when filming can and can't happen.
  9. Sign-off. Who approves the film, named, from the start.
  10. Constraints. What can't be shown, brand guidelines, legal or compliance checks, accessibility needs.
  11. References. Two or three films you like, and why. One you don't, and why.

What do most video briefs get wrong?

They describe the answer. "Two minutes, upbeat music, drone shot of the building, MD to camera, make it engaging." That's a brief for a film you've already imagined, and it tells the production company nothing about the problem it's meant to solve. You'll get exactly what you asked for, and it might not work.

A related mistake is copying a competitor's film into the brief. If theirs worked, it worked for their goal and their audience, and a lookalike will just make you sound like them, which is the one thing a brand film should never do.

The other common gaps are no budget, no clear audience ("everyone" isn't an audience) and no named person signing it off. That last one causes more pain than any other, because a senior voice arriving at the final cut can undo weeks of work.

A brief that describes the answer gets you exactly what you asked for, and it might not work.

Compare that with what can happen when a brief starts from the problem. With the Easee brand films, the starting point was simple: nobody wakes up wanting a charge point. They want one because something else happened. So instead of one film about the product, there were three, each built around a moment that actually triggers a purchase: moving house, passing your test, and being a landlord with a grant to claim.

How much creative direction should you give?

Less than you think, and more context than you think. Give the problem and the non-negotiables, then let the company come back with an approach. That's what you're paying them for.

References are the exception, and they're useful. "We like this because it feels unhurried" or "this one, because the customer does all the talking" tells a director more than a page of adjectives. Say what you don't want as well. It's often the quickest way to rule out the wrong direction.

If your brief says "make it go viral", I'll take that as a sign we need a longer call.

For documentary-style work there's another reason to hold back. The real story usually turns up during research, in conversations with your people. If the brief has already fixed the script, there's nowhere for it to go.

How do you brief for a film where you can't show everything?

Say so in the brief, early. It changes how the whole thing gets shot. On the Car Planet customer story, the client didn't want the site itself on display. Knowing that in advance meant framing everything tight on the work and planning to fill the edit with b-roll from previous installs and the client's own image bank. Finding out on the day would have been a very different story.

The same goes for anything confidential: customer names, pricing on screens, staff who can't appear, areas that need permission to film. None of it is a problem if it's known up front.

How long should a video brief be?

One to two pages. Long enough to cover the eleven points above, short enough that the person who signs it off will actually read it. If it's running to five, it's probably trying to brief two films at once, and it's worth asking whether you need two films. Write it in plain language, the way you'd explain it to someone over coffee. A brief that only makes sense to people inside your business won't make sense to the people you're hiring.

What happens after you send the brief?

A good production company will come back with questions, and maybe some pushback. That's a good sign. It means they've read it properly and are thinking about whether the approach suits the goal. Be wary of the opposite, a polished proposal back within the hour that could have been written for anyone.

With us, the brief starts the research stage. We spend time with you before anything's filmed, and come back with the story we think it is, so you can tell us whether we're right. Then the project is quoted as one fixed figure, agreed before anything's booked. You can see the full process on our films page, and if you need to set the number first, start with how to set a video budget.

If you'd like a fuller planning template, our free 44-page guide Before the camera comes out covers the whole thing. And if your brief is already written, send it over. We come back within one working day.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should a video brief include a script?
faqs.a: Usually not for documentary-style work. A script fixes the story before anyone has done the research, and real people reading lines tend to sound like they're reading lines. For explainers, training videos or anything with precise information to get across, a script can be the right tool. Even then, share the key messages in the brief and let the production company help shape the wording.

faqs.q: Who should write the video brief?
faqs.a: Whoever owns the goal the film serves, usually the marketing lead or the founder. They don't need to write it alone. Get input from sales, HR or whoever will actually use the film, and agree it with the person who'll sign it off. One clear owner stops the brief turning into a list of everyone's wishes pulling in different directions.

faqs.q: What if we don't know what kind of video we need?
faqs.a: Then write the brief around the problem and leave the format open. Describe the goal, the audience and where you'd like it to be seen, and ask the production company to recommend an approach. A good one will tell you if you need a documentary, a case study, a run of short pieces or something else entirely, and will say so if video isn't the answer.

faqs.q: How far in advance should you brief a production company?
faqs.a: For a documentary-style brand film, six to ten weeks before you need it at the very least, because research and editing can't be rushed. If there's a fixed date like a launch or an event, add a few weeks for availability and sign-off. Simpler content can move faster, but a rushed brief usually costs more than it saves.
