items.title: How wireless audio works for interviews
items.excerpt: How wireless mics work for interviews: transmitters, receivers, UK frequencies, what causes dropouts, why you record a backup and why someone always listens.
items.coverAlt: A small crew filming on set with lights and a camera rig
items.body:
A wireless mic system is two boxes. A transmitter on the speaker's belt, with a lav mic plugged into it, turns the voice into a radio signal, and a receiver on the camera or sound recorder turns it back into audio. It means nobody's tied to the camera by a cable. It also means you're relying on a radio link, which is why any decent crew records a backup and listens on headphones the entire time.

Wireless kit has got smaller and cheaper over the last few years, to the point where plenty of people filming on their own now own a set. That's good news. The radio side still behaves like radio, though, and knowing roughly how it works is the difference between a clean interview and forty minutes of something you can't use.

How does a wireless microphone work?

The transmitter is a small pack, usually clipped to a belt or the back of a waistband, with the lav cable running up under the shirt to the chest. Some newer compact systems build the microphone into the transmitter itself, so the whole thing clips straight onto clothing. The transmitter sends the audio out on a radio frequency.

The receiver sits on the camera or feeds a separate sound recorder. It's tuned to the same frequency as the transmitter, picks up the signal and passes the audio into the recording. One receiver can often take two transmitters, which is handy for two-person interviews.

There are two broad families. Analogue systems have been the standard for decades and usually work in the UHF range. Digital systems convert the audio to data before sending it, which tends to sound cleaner, at the cost of a very small delay. Many compact digital systems work at 2.4GHz, the same band used by wifi and Bluetooth, which matters for the next part.

What frequencies do wireless mics use in the UK?

Radio spectrum in the UK is managed by Ofcom, and wireless mics have to stay inside the bands they're allowed to use. According to Ofcom's guidance on wireless microphones, the ranges 173.8 to 175 MHz, 863 to 865 MHz and 2400 to 2483.5 MHz can be used without a licence, but they're shared with other low-power equipment and so are open to interference. Other UHF frequencies need a licence, and coordinated licences for a specific site give the best protection.

In plain terms, the licence-free bands are busy. Wifi routers, phones, wireless speakers and other people's mics are all in there with you. Kit bought abroad may also be set to frequencies that aren't allowed here, so check it's sold for UK use. If a crew is working somewhere with heavy radio traffic, like a big event or a city centre office, licensed frequencies are part of how they keep the link clean.

What causes interference and dropouts?

A dropout is a moment where the receiver loses the signal and the audio cuts, crackles or goes digital and glitchy. The usual causes are worth knowing because most of them are easy to avoid:

  • Other devices on the same frequency. Most receivers can scan for a clear channel. Do it at the location, not at home.
  • The human body. We're mostly water, and water soaks up radio signal. A transmitter on someone's back with the receiver in front of them is working through a person.
  • Distance and obstacles. Walls, metal shelving, cars and fridges all weaken the signal. Keep a clear line between transmitter and receiver where you can.
  • Too many systems at once. Several transmitters close together can interfere with each other, especially in the narrow licence-free bands.
  • Batteries. As they run down, range shrinks and dropouts start. Fresh or fully charged batteries at the start of every interview, not halfway through.

A flat battery never goes during the boring bit. It waits for the best answer of the day, then it goes.

Why record a backup?

Because a radio link can fail and you won't always know straight away. Plenty of current transmitters can record the audio internally as well as sending it, which means even if the signal drops, there's a clean copy sitting on the pack. Others use a separate small recorder on the speaker. Either way, the backup gets lined up with the main recording in the edit, using timecode or by matching the sound waves.

Some crews also record a second safety track on the main recorder, the same voice set a little quieter, so if someone suddenly shouts or laughs, there's a version that didn't clip. Newer recorders that work in 32-bit float handle loud peaks far better, but the backup copy is still worth having. I'd treat any interview you can't easily reshoot, and that's most of them, as one that needs two copies of the voice.

A wireless link is a radio, and radios drop out. Plan for the moment it does.

Why does someone need to wear headphones the whole time?

Because the meters only tell you how loud something is. They don't tell you what it is. A recording can sit at a perfect level and still be full of shirt rustle, a fridge hum, a buzz from a nearby cable or a dropout that lasted half a second. You only catch those by listening, and you only fix them on the day if you hear them on the day.

Whoever's monitoring should be listening to what's actually being recorded, through closed-back headphones that block out the room. The things they're listening for:

  • Rustle and taps from clothing or hands
  • Crackle, cuts or glitches that mean the signal's struggling
  • Background noise that's crept up, like traffic, aircon or a phone on silent buzzing on the table
  • A voice that's gone muffled because the mic has slipped under a fold of shirt

When they hear something, they stop the interview at a natural pause and fix it. It's mildly awkward for a second. It's a lot less awkward than discovering in the edit that the best story of the day has a dropout through the middle of it.

Our La Fromagerie film was shot in shops that were open and trading, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. Busy locations like that are where sound needs the most attention: tills, chatter, fridges and people walking between the camera and whoever's talking.

Is wireless always better than a cable?

No. For a sit-down interview where nobody's moving, a wired mic is the most reliable thing you can use, because there's no radio to go wrong. Wireless earns its place when people are walking, working or moving around a space, when the camera needs to be some distance away, or when a cable across the floor would be a trip hazard or end up in shot.

For a brand documentary, where the good material often comes from people doing their actual work rather than sitting in a chair, wireless is usually part of the kit. It just needs the backup and the headphones to go with it. If you're weighing up which mic to put on someone in the first place, start with lav mics explained, and if you want the bigger picture of what goes into planning a shoot, our free guide covers what happens before the camera comes out.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do you need a licence for wireless microphones in the UK?
faqs.a: Not always. Ofcom allows some bands, including 863 to 865 MHz and 2400 to 2483.5 MHz, to be used without a licence, though they're shared and open to interference. Other UHF frequencies need an Ofcom licence. Check that any system you buy is sold for UK use, because kit from other countries can be set to frequencies that aren't permitted here.

faqs.q: How far can a wireless mic transmit?
faqs.a: It depends on the system, the frequency and what's in the way. Manufacturers quote ranges in open space, and real locations are rarely that kind. Walls, metal, crowds and the speaker's own body all cut the range, sometimes sharply. For interviews, keep the receiver reasonably close with a clear line to the transmitter, and you'll avoid most dropouts.

faqs.q: Is a digital wireless mic better than analogue?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Digital systems tend to sound cleaner and are often smaller and easier to set up, but they add a tiny delay and many share the busy 2.4GHz band with wifi. Analogue UHF systems are long proven and can be very reliable when set up well. The right choice depends on where you're filming and how many systems you need at once.

faqs.q: Can you fix a wireless dropout in the edit?
faqs.a: Usually only if there's a backup recording. A dropout means the audio was never recorded cleanly, so there's nothing to repair. If the transmitter recorded internally, or a second mic was running, the editor can swap in that version for the damaged section. Without one, the options are cutting around it, asking for the line again, or living with it.

items.title: Brand documentary vs corporate video: what changes
items.excerpt: Brand documentary vs corporate video: who speaks, scripted versus found stories, no voice of god, and why that changes how much viewers trust you.
items.coverAlt: The Barry Road homeowner talking on camera in the finished living room
items.body:
A corporate video is usually scripted, presented by the company and often narrated, so it tells you what the business wants you to think. A brand documentary is built from real people telling their own story in their own words, with no narrator reading lines over the top, and it leaves the viewer to make up their own mind. That's why people tend to believe a documentary and tune out a corporate video.

Most corporate videos follow a pattern you'd recognise with the sound off. A managing director reading lines to camera. A narrator telling you the company is passionate about quality. A drone shot of the building, a few people pointing at screens, and music that builds towards the logo. You've seen hundreds of them. I'd be surprised if you could remember one.

A brand documentary often uses the same kit, and sometimes a similar budget. What changes is how it's made, and the viewer picks up on that in the first few seconds. Here are the differences that matter, using films we've made.

Who speaks in a brand documentary?

In a corporate video the company speaks about itself. The MD, the head of sales, a hired presenter, or a narrator nobody ever sees. Everything said is something the business wants you to believe, and the viewer knows it.

In a documentary the story is told by the people who lived it. Sometimes that's the founder. Often it's the people who work there, or the customer.

Our Barry Road film is a good example. A London builder had taken on a full renovation in East Dulwich. Every contractor says the same things about themselves: quality, on time, on budget. None of it carries much weight coming from the person being paid. So the film is the homeowner's account, in their own words, filmed once the family had moved back in. The builder barely needs to appear.

We did the same on Nimrod Road in Tooting. A Victorian house that had sat empty, a project that started in September, and a couple with a baby due at the end of November. They tell it. Someone weighing up the same decision hears it from a person in their own position, and that's the version most people believe.

Is a brand documentary scripted?

Corporate video usually starts with a script. Somebody writes it, a few people approve it, and then real people are asked to say it out loud on camera. Even a good script sounds like a script once a non-actor reads it.

Mostly no. Documentary starts with research. We spend time with the business before filming, work out what the story actually is, and then go and film conversations. The structure gets found in the interviews and in the edit, which is why the edit takes as long as it does.

When we made the La Fromagerie film, the story was already sitting there. A wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed. A market stall at Camden Lock and a shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week. Thirty three years on, three shops with walk-in cheese rooms and a wholesale business supplying restaurants across London. Nobody had to write that. The founder told it, and the cheesemongers and the wholesale side filled in what the business is now. Four people's accounts of the same business in one film, which a script would have flattened into a single voice.

What is "voice of god" narration, and why leave it out?

"Voice of god" is the industry name for the narrator you never see. Deep, calm, slightly too pleased with the company. It's efficient, because it lets you say anything in any order. That's also why viewers have learned to tune it out. It's obviously the company talking through a hired voice.

If your film needs a stranger with a deep voice to tell people you’re trustworthy, that’s worth a second thought.

Without a narrator, everything has to come from someone on screen. That's harder to make and far more convincing to watch. On Carreducker, Deborah Carre and James Ducker met as apprentices under the same master shoemaker at John Lobb, and later set up on their own. They finish each other's sentences, so we shot the interview as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts instead of two takes cut together. A few seconds of them talking over each other tells you more about how that business works than a minute of narration could.

Why do brand documentaries feel slower?

Corporate edits tend to be fast. Every second has to justify itself, so the cuts come quickly and music fills any gap. For a ninety second explainer that's fine.

A documentary leaves room. A pause before someone answers. The work happening at the speed it actually happens. With Signwriting Jack, the whole point is the hand: the brush loading, and a single unbroken line that either works or doesn't. Chop that into half-second shots and you've thrown away the only thing worth watching. So we filmed close, waited, and let the shots run.

Slow, done well, reads as confidence. The film isn't in a hurry to sell you anything, so you settle in and keep watching.

Why film real people in real places?

Corporate shoots often happen after hours, in a cleared office, with everyone asked to act natural. Documentary goes where the business actually lives, while it's running. La Fromagerie was filmed during trading hours, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. Catherine Marche was filmed at her bench and in a glass fronted shop, where reflections and mixed light fight you the whole way. It's harder work. It also looks like the place you'd actually walk into, and that counts when someone's deciding whether to trust you.

Same with the people. Nothing read off an autocue, and nobody asked to do it again with more energy. When the person on screen is the person a customer would actually deal with, the film does something a presenter can't.

Why does the difference matter to the viewer?

Someone watching a corporate video is being told things. Someone watching a documentary is working things out for themselves, and people trust a conclusion they've reached on their own far more than one handed to them. I think that's most of it. It's why these films get watched to the end and passed on, and why they still hold up years later.

People can tell when they’re being sold to. They lean in when they’re being told something.

It matters most where trust is what's actually being bought. The price is high, people research before they commit, and the competition all sound identical on paper.

Does a brand documentary still need a business goal?

It does, and this is where a lot of lovely films fall down. Being honest and well shot isn't enough on its own. If nobody decided what the film was for, it gets a round of compliments, sits on the website and does very little.

The Barry Road film has a plain job. It's an edit the builder can send to a prospective client who's deciding whether to trust them with a house. The London Fight Factory seminar film was cut as a highlight edit the gym can use to sell the next one. Knowing that before the shoot changed what we filmed and how we cut it. So when someone asks me for a documentary, the first thing I want to talk about is the goal it serves and the budget behind it, and I'd rather we were both straight about both from the start.

When is corporate video the better choice?

To be fair to it, plenty of jobs suit a scripted corporate video. Internal training, compliance, a product walkthrough, anything where getting precise information across matters more than how the viewer feels. A script is the right tool there, and a documentary would be the slow, expensive way round.

But if there's a founder with a story, a craft that took years to learn, or a customer whose life changed because of you, that's a film. You can see the ones we've made on our films page, and if you think your business has one in it, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Does a brand documentary cost more than a corporate video?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, though the gap is often smaller than people expect. Both can use the same kit and sometimes a similar budget. The extra cost sits in research before the shoot, more shoot days so people relax on camera, and far longer in the edit, because the story gets found in the interviews. In the UK most corporate video sits between £2,000 and £8,000, and documentary brand films typically land between £8,000 and £30,000.

faqs.q: Can a B2B company use a brand documentary?
faqs.a: Yes, and it often suits B2B better than consumer brands. Documentary works hardest where trust is what's being bought, the price is high, buyers research before they commit and every competitor sounds the same on paper. That describes a lot of B2B. Your engineers, your team or a customer explaining the work in their own words will carry more weight with a careful buyer than any presenter or narrator could.

faqs.q: How do you get customers to appear in a brand documentary?
faqs.a: You ask the ones who had a genuinely good experience and are happy to talk about it. It helps to film once the result is real, like a family already back in their finished house, and to keep it a conversation with no script to learn. Get their written consent to appear, which is standard on any shoot. A customer telling their own story is the version prospective buyers believe.

faqs.q: Can a brand documentary be used on social media and in ads?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the shoot's planned for it. The main documentary usually runs four to ten minutes, which suits a website, YouTube, events and sales conversations. From the same footage we cut a sixty to ninety second version and six to ten vertical pieces made for the feed. Before you put money behind any of it, check your licence covers paid advertising and the music licence covers every platform you'll use.

stat.title: Who people trust to tell them the truth about a brand
stat.takeaway: People believe customers and staff more than the person at the top, so a film built on real voices will land harder than a polished company message.

source.name: Edelman, 2025 Edelman Trust Barometer Special Report: Brand Trust, From We to Me (15 markets, 15,000+ respondents)

items.title: What cinematography means, and why it moves you
items.excerpt: What cinematography actually means: how framing, light, lenses, camera movement and colour grading shape the way a film makes you feel, in plain English.
items.coverAlt: Two men by a fire at golden hour above a fjord
items.body:
Cinematography is every decision about how a film looks: where the camera sits, what's in the frame, how it's lit, which lens is on, whether the camera moves, and what colour the final image ends up. It's why two films of the same person saying the same words can feel completely different. Good cinematography makes those choices on purpose, so they push the viewer towards a feeling without them noticing they're being pushed.

Most people can't say why a film moved them. They just know it did. Here's what's going on underneath, in plain terms, so you know what you're looking at when you watch a film and what you're paying for when you commission one.

What does a cinematographer actually do?

On a big production, the cinematographer, also called the director of photography or DP, is in charge of the image. They work with the director on the look, then lead the camera and lighting teams to get it. On a smaller documentary shoot, one person might direct, operate the camera and light the room. The job is the same either way: turning what's in front of the camera into pictures that tell the story.

A lot of it happens before filming starts. Looking at the locations, deciding how the film should feel, picking lenses, planning where the interviews will sit. On the day it's mostly a long run of small decisions, made fast.

How does framing change how you feel about someone?

Framing is what's in the shot and where it sits. A few choices carry a lot of weight:

  • Shot size. A wide shows a person in their world. A mid shot is conversation distance. A close-up puts you near enough to see someone think, which is where a lot of emotion lives in an interview.
  • Where the person sits in the frame. Off to one side, with space in the direction they're looking, feels natural and open. Dead centre, with symmetry, feels formal or deliberate. Squeezed against the edge with empty space behind them can feel uneasy or lonely.
  • Camera height. Eye level feels equal. A camera looking up at someone can make them feel bigger, and looking down can make them feel smaller.
  • Eye-line. In documentary, the speaker usually looks just off the lens at the interviewer, which feels like you're overhearing a real conversation. Straight down the lens feels more direct, more like a presenter.

What does light do to the mood?

Light decides where the eye goes and how a scene feels. Bright, even light with soft shadows feels open and safe. Darker images with deep shadows and pools of light feel intimate, serious or dramatic. A lot of good documentary uses motivated light, meaning light that seems to come from a real source in the scene, like a window or a lamp, so it feels honest rather than staged. I've gone through the basics in interview lighting explained simply.

Nobody has ever been moved to tears by a drone shot of a business park. It's still in almost every corporate video.

Why does lens choice matter?

Lenses don't just zoom in or out. They change how space looks. A wide lens close to someone puts you in the room with them, with lots of the environment around them, and gets a bit distorted if you go too close to a face. A long lens from further back compresses the space, so the background looks closer and bigger, and isolates the person from everything else.

Then there's depth of field, how much of the image is sharp. A shallow depth of field, where the person is sharp and the background melts into blur, pulls your attention onto them. It's lovely in moderation, but it's become a cliche. Every food advert now is a blurry background, a pair of hands and a voiceover. Deeper focus, where you can see the room, tells you more about where someone lives and works, and in documentary that context is often the point.

I tend to prefer mixing focal lengths in an edit. Wide for the place, mid for the conversation, close for the detail and the emotion. Cutting between them gives the viewer's eye somewhere new to land without the film feeling jumpy.

When should the camera move?

When there's a reason. A camera that moves for no reason feels restless, and viewers pick that up even if they can't say why. Movement that follows something, like a slow push in as someone gets to the heart of a story, or the camera drifting with a craftsperson's hands across a bench, feels natural.

A locked-off camera feels calm and observant. It lets the person do the work. Handheld feels closer and more alive, with a little energy and imperfection in it. Gimbal and slider moves feel smooth and considered. None of them is better in itself. The question is always what the moment needs, which is also why the kit choices, down to what the camera's sitting on, matter more than they look.

Two films of the same person saying the same words can feel completely different.

What is colour grading?

Colour grading is the last stage of the picture, where the colour, brightness and contrast of every shot are adjusted in the edit. It happens in two parts.

Colour correction comes first. It fixes problems and makes shots match: balancing white so skin looks like skin, evening out exposure, and making sure a shot from the morning sits next to one from the afternoon without a jump. A lot of cameras record in a flat, washed out profile called log, which keeps as much detail as possible for the grade. Straight out of the camera it looks grey and lifeless. Correction is what turns it back into a normal image.

The grade is the creative part. Warmer or cooler, softer or punchier, richer or more muted. You'll hear about LUTs, which are preset looks applied to footage, often used as a starting point. A grade can make a workshop feel warm and familiar, or a city feel cold and lonely, and it's a big part of why some films look expensive and others look like video. Skin tones are the priority throughout. If people look ill or orange, the grade's gone wrong, however stylish the rest is. On our films the grade is done by specialists, because it's not a corner worth cutting.

Why do some films make you feel something?

Because all of these choices point the same way. The framing, the light, the lens, the movement and the colour are all agreeing with each other and with the story, so nothing pulls you out and everything nudges you in.

With La Fromagerie, the brief we set ourselves was to avoid the usual food film, the one shot like an advert with shallow focus, hands, a voiceover and nobody in it. It's four people's accounts of one business, filmed in open shops and in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. The look has to serve the people and the place, not the other way round.

Cinematography can't rescue a film with nothing to say. That part comes from research, access and the story, which is what our free guide is about. But when the story's there, the pictures are what make someone feel it. If you think your business has a film in it, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What's the difference between a cinematographer and a camera operator?
faqs.a: A cinematographer designs and leads the look of the film, including lighting, lenses and framing. A camera operator physically runs the camera to get the shots. On large productions they're different people, and the operator works to the cinematographer's plan. On smaller documentary shoots one person often does both, and sometimes directs as well.

faqs.q: Does a more expensive camera make a film look more cinematic?
faqs.a: Less than most people think. A better camera gives more detail, cleaner low light performance and more room in the grade. But the cinematic feel comes mostly from light, framing, lens choice, movement and the grade. A well lit, well framed shot on a modest camera will beat a badly lit shot on an expensive one every time.

faqs.q: What is a LUT in colour grading?
faqs.a: A LUT, short for look-up table, is a file that converts the colours of footage from one set of values to another. It's often used to turn flat log footage into a normal looking image, or to apply a preset creative look. Colourists usually treat a LUT as a starting point, then adjust shot by shot so everything matches and skin tones stay natural.

faqs.q: How long does colour grading take?
faqs.a: It depends on the length of the film, the number of shots and how much matching is needed. A short social edit might take a few hours. A documentary of several minutes, shot across different days and locations, can take a day or more, because every shot has to match its neighbours before any creative look goes on top.

items.title: La Fromagerie: the story behind a documentary brand film
items.excerpt: How we made a documentary brand film for La Fromagerie, a London cheese business that started in a garden shed, and what we chose to show and why.
items.coverAlt: The founder of La Fromagerie talking on camera in her shop
items.body:
A documentary brand film is a film about a business told by the people who run it, in the place where they work, cut as a story rather than an advert. The example I send people most is La Fromagerie, a London cheese business that started with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed. Thirty three years later it's three shops with walk-in cheese rooms and a wholesale side supplying restaurants across London, and the film lets four of the people behind it tell you how.

This is the story behind that film. How it came together, what we chose to put in it, what we steered away from, and why. If you run a small business and you're trying to picture what a film could look like for you, it's a decent place to start.

What is La Fromagerie?

The founder tells the beginning herself, and it's about as unglamorous as starts get. A market stall at Camden Lock. A shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week. A wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed.

From there to three shops, each with its own walk-in cheese room, plus a wholesale business that supplies restaurants across London. That's thirty three years of work, and you can't squeeze it into a sixty second advert without losing most of it.

It's also why we didn't make a film about cheese. The cheese is beautiful, obviously. But a film made of cheese close-ups tells you very little about why a business is still going after three decades, or who's behind it.

Why didn't we shoot it like a food advert?

Most food films are shot as adverts. Shallow depth of field, hands, a voiceover, and nobody actually in them. I'll be honest, I find most of them a bit forgettable. They look lovely. You could also swap the logo at the end and the same film would work for pretty much any deli in the country.

I wanted this one to go the other way. People on camera, talking in their own words, in the place where they actually work. If you'd never heard of La Fromagerie before, I wanted you to come away knowing who runs it, how it started, and what it's like now.

That's the whole idea behind how we make our films. Real conversations, real places, nothing read off an autocue, and enough room in the edit for the thing to breathe.

Why does the film have four voices instead of one?

The founder carries the origin story. She was there for the market stall and the shed, so nobody else could tell that part. But a business that's grown to three shops and a wholesale operation has a lot more people in it than one, and a film that only showed the founder would've told half the story.

So we interviewed the cheesemongers and the wholesale side as well. Four people's accounts of the same business. The founder gives you where it came from. The cheesemongers and the wholesale team fill in what it actually is today.

The hard part was stopping that from turning into a corporate video. Four people taking it in turns to say their bit is exactly the format I was trying to avoid. The edit had to hold several voices at once without feeling like a round of introductions at a team meeting.

That's a structure problem more than a picture problem. In our edits structure comes first, then pace, then picture, and on a film like this it's where the real decisions get made.

Why more than one voice helps a small business

If you're a founder, it's tempting to be the whole film. You know the story better than anyone. I get it.

But the people thinking about buying from you, and the people you might want to hire, want a sense of what it's like on the other side of the counter too. Hearing from the team shows there's more to the place than one person, and that it carries on when you're not in the room. A single voice can't really show that, however good the interview is.

Why film while the shops were open?

We filmed during trading hours, around customers, rather than waiting for the shutters to come down. That was a choice, and it made the job harder.

Cheese rooms are cold, dark and full of people. Three things a camera hates and a cheesemonger doesn’t mind at all.

The cheese rooms are cold and dark. When the shops are open they're full of customers. You can't take over a working shop the way you'd take over an empty set, and nobody wants a crew in the way while someone's trying to buy cheese.

But a shop filmed after hours looks like a shop after hours. Empty, tidy and a bit lifeless. La Fromagerie is a place people come into and get served, and if you film it closed you lose the part that makes it a shop at all.

So the coverage moves through the shops, the cheese rooms and the counter while the business carries on around it. It's less controlled than a closed set. I think it's more honest for it, and honesty is most of what you're paying for with this kind of film.

What did we choose to show, and why?

Every film is a long list of decisions about what goes in. These were the ones that mattered here.

The most interesting thing about a business is usually the thing nobody’s filmed yet.
  • The founder at the counter in her own shop. It's the frame we used as the cover for the case study, and it sums the film up. She isn't in a studio or in front of a backdrop. She's where she works.
  • The cheese rooms. Walk-in cheese rooms are a big part of what the shops are, so they had to be in it, cold and dark as they are.
  • The cheesemongers. They're the people a customer actually deals with, so their account of the business carries real weight.
  • The wholesale side. Supplying restaurants across London is part of what La Fromagerie is now, and a film about the shops alone would've missed it.

What we steered away from was the advert version: a narrator over beautiful close-ups, with nobody in shot. There's a place for that kind of thing. It just doesn't tell you anything about the people, and the people are the reason this business is worth a film.

What makes a small business brand film work?

I don't think you need thirty three years and three shops to have a film in you. What you need is a real story and people willing to tell it on camera.

When I'm researching a film, I'm looking for the person who started it, the part of the job nobody outside gets to see, and the people who make it work every day. At La Fromagerie that was the founder, the cheese rooms and the counter, and the team behind both the shops and the wholesale.

The other thing I'd take from this one is to let the business be itself on the day. Open, busy, a bit cold, customers in the background. Viewers can tell when a place has been dressed up for the camera, and they can tell when it hasn't.

A garden shed, a market stall and an eighty pound a week shop aren't the kind of start most companies would put in their marketing. Here they're the heart of the film, told by the person who lived it, with the people who run it alongside her filling in the rest.

You can watch it on the La Fromagerie case study. If you want to know how we make films like this, from research to the final mix, it's all on the films page, and if you think your business has a story in it, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a small business with one shop have a documentary brand film?
faqs.a: Yes. You don't need thirty three years and three shops to have a film in you. What you need is a real story and people willing to tell it on camera: how it started, the part of the job nobody outside gets to see, or a customer who took a chance on you. A single shop with a founder who really cares about the craft has more than enough for a film.

faqs.q: How many people should be interviewed for a brand film?
faqs.a: As many as it takes to tell the whole story, and usually fewer than you'd think. For La Fromagerie it was four: the founder for the origin story, then the cheesemongers and the wholesale team for what the business is now. A one person business might need one voice plus a customer. Every extra voice has to add something new, or the edit starts to feel like a round of introductions.

faqs.q: Will filming disrupt my customers on the day?
faqs.a: Very little, if the crew is small and the day's planned properly. We filmed La Fromagerie during trading hours, around customers, and the shops carried on as normal. A small crew works around the business, waits for the right moment and keeps out of the way of anyone trying to buy something. Customers who'd end up clearly in shot need to be happy to appear, so we ask them first.

faqs.q: Where should a small business use its brand film?
faqs.a: Wherever someone's deciding whether to trust you. That usually means the full film on your website, YouTube, in sales conversations, at events and for recruitment, a sixty to ninety second cut at the top of the homepage, and vertical pieces on social. Decide the main job before filming, because it changes who's in it and how it's cut. A film with no job tends to sit on the About page doing nothing.

items.title: Interview lighting explained simply
items.excerpt: Key, fill and back light explained in plain English, plus practicals, lighting with a window, mixed colours and why one big soft light often looks best.
items.coverAlt: A softly lit interview in a bright room
items.body:
Interview lighting is usually built from three lights. A key light does most of the work on the face, a fill light softens the shadows it leaves, and a back light separates the person from the background. Practicals, the lamps you can see in the shot, and windows fill in the rest. And very often, the interviews that look best use one big, soft light source and not much else.

You don't need to know any of this to commission a film. It helps, though, when someone on a shoot spends forty minutes moving a light about a foot to the left and you're wondering what you're paying for. Here's what they're doing.

What is three-point lighting?

It's the basic setup taught on every film course, and most interview lighting is a variation on it.

Key light

The main light, and the one that decides the look. It usually sits to one side of the camera, roughly forty-five degrees off the line between camera and subject, and a little above eye height. Where it goes sets which side of the face is bright and which side falls into shadow.

A small detail that makes a big difference: most cinematographers put the key on the far side of the face, the side turned away from camera. It's called short lighting, and it gives a face more shape. Light the side nearest camera instead and the face tends to look flatter and wider.

Fill light

The fill sits on the other side and lifts the shadows the key leaves behind. How much fill you use sets the contrast. Lots of fill gives an even, bright look that suits corporate work. Very little gives more drama and a moodier feel. The fill doesn't have to be a light at all. A white board or a reflector bouncing some of the key back works fine, and sometimes the right amount of fill is none. Some crews even do the opposite, putting black fabric on the fill side to deepen the shadow, which is called negative fill.

Back light

A light behind the subject, usually high and opposite the key, that catches the edge of the hair and shoulders. It draws a thin line around the person so they don't melt into a dark background. Used gently, nobody notices it. Overdone, it looks like a halo in a shampoo advert.

What are practicals, and why do they matter?

A practical is any light source you can see in the frame: a desk lamp, a pendant over a counter, fairy lights, the glow of a fridge in a cheese room. They do two jobs. They make the background look like a real, lived-in place instead of a black void or a flat wall, and they give a reason for the light falling on the subject, so the whole image feels motivated rather than set up.

Practicals are also one of the cheapest ways to make an interview look expensive. A warm lamp glowing out of focus over the speaker's shoulder adds depth and colour for the price of a bulb. The usual trick is swapping in a dimmable bulb so the practical sits at the right brightness and doesn't blow out.

Overhead office lighting was designed so nobody trips over a bin. It was never meant to make anyone look like they've slept.

Can you light an interview with a window?

Yes, and a big window is one of the best soft light sources there is. Sit the person side-on or at an angle to it, so the window becomes the key light, and use a reflector or a white wall on the other side as fill. Overcast days are a gift, because the cloud diffuses the sun into an even, flattering light.

A few things go wrong with windows:

  • Direct sun. Hard, bright patches and squinting. Hang a net curtain or a sheet of diffusion over the glass to soften it.
  • Back to the window. The camera exposes for the bright sky and the person turns into a silhouette. Unless you add light to the front, turn them round.
  • Changing weather. This is the big one for interviews. A cloud goes over halfway through an answer and the light on the face changes. In the edit, two parts of the same answer no longer match. Crews who rely on daylight keep an eye on the sky, and often add a light of their own to keep things steady.

Why does one big soft light often look best?

Because softness comes from the size of the light compared to the person, and soft light is kind to faces. A small, bare bulb throws hard shadows with crisp edges and shows every line and blemish. A large source, like a big window, a light fired through a large diffusion panel or bounced off a white wall, wraps around the face. The shadows fade gently instead of stopping dead.

Distance matters too. The closer a soft light is to the subject, the bigger it is relative to them and the softer it gets. It also falls off faster, so the background drops darker, which is often exactly what you want. One big source close to the face, a bit of negative fill on the other side and a practical in the background is a setup you'll see on a lot of very good interviews.

The light you choose tells the viewer how to feel about someone before they've said a word.

It's also quicker. Fewer lights means less time rigging, fewer stands in a cramped room and fewer things to go wrong, which matters when you're filming in somebody's working business rather than a studio.

What happens when light sources don't match?

Different lights have different colours. Daylight is cool and bluish. Household bulbs and old-style tungsten lamps are warm and orange. Fluorescent tubes can tip green. Cameras can balance for one colour at a time, so a face lit by a window on one side and a warm lamp on the other can look like it's half in two different rooms.

Sometimes that mix is a deliberate choice, like a cool daylight key with a warm practical in the background. Often it's just a mess. Crews deal with it by turning off the lights they don't want, matching their own lights to the main source, or putting coloured gel over a light to bring it into line.

Our film for Catherine Marche was shot in a working studio and a glass fronted shop, where reflections and mixed lighting fight you the whole way. That's normal for documentary. You don't get to pick the room, so the lighting has to work with the place as it is.

What does this mean for your film?

Lighting takes time on a shoot day, and that time is part of what you're paying for. Good crews light the space before anyone sits down, then refine it with the person in the chair, so your team isn't waiting around under hot lights. If you're filming on your own, start with the window, turn off the overheads, add a lamp in the background, and you'll be ahead of most office videos. If you want to know how lighting fits into the bigger picture of how a film looks and feels, I've written about that in what cinematography actually means.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What's the best single light for filming interviews?
faqs.a: A large, soft source placed close to the speaker and slightly to one side. That could be a big window, or a light fired through a large diffusion panel or softbox. Size relative to the person is what makes light soft and flattering. If you only have one light, make it big and soft, then use a white wall or reflector on the other side for fill.

faqs.q: Should you use ring lights for interviews?
faqs.a: They're fine for talking to camera on calls and social clips, but they're rarely the best choice for a filmed interview. A ring light sits right by the lens and lights the face from the front, which flattens it and puts a ring-shaped reflection in the eyes. Light from the side gives a face more shape and looks more natural on screen.

faqs.q: Why do faces look orange or blue on camera?
faqs.a: Because the camera's white balance doesn't match the light hitting the face. Daylight is bluish and household bulbs are warm. When the camera is set for one and the face is lit by the other, skin goes blue or orange. Mixed sources cause both at once. Setting white balance to the main light, and switching off competing lights, usually fixes it.

faqs.q: How long does lighting an interview take?
faqs.a: Anything from fifteen minutes for a simple window setup to well over an hour for a complex location with several lights. It depends on the room, the look and how many angles are being shot. Most crews light before the speaker arrives, using a stand-in, then fine-tune for a few minutes once the person is in the chair.

items.title: How to prepare for being filmed for a brand film
items.excerpt: Never been filmed before? What to wear, how the interview works, what happens on the day and how to handle nerves when you're filmed for a brand film.
items.coverAlt: A nervous man in a suit reading a statement in front of a bedsheet, like a hostage video, with a film camera in the foreground
items.body:
You don't need to learn anything to be filmed for a brand film. Wear plain, mid-tone clothes you'd normally work in, think of a few stories about your job, tidy the clutter but leave the place looking like itself, and turn up. The interview is a conversation, you can restart any answer as many times as you like, and we edit out everything that doesn't work.

That's the short version. Most of the people we film have never been filmed before. Founders, shop staff, tradespeople, the person who's run the warehouse for years and would rather be anywhere else that morning. Nearly all of them are nervous, and nearly all of them are fine once we get going.

If you've booked a film and someone on your team is dreading it, forward them this.

Do I need to learn a script?

This is the bit that relaxes people most, so it goes first. There's no autocue and no lines to learn. The interview is a conversation. I ask questions, you answer them the way you'd explain something to a friend who's genuinely interested, and we follow the good bits wherever they go.

It’s a conversation, not a performance. If you fluff a line, you just say it again.

Please don't write your answers out and memorise them. People who do that sound like they're reading, even when they're not. It's much better to think about a few stories beforehand. How you started. A day that went wrong. A customer you remember. The part of your job you're proudest of. Then let the questions bring them out.

Answer in full sentences

This is the one practical habit worth practising. My questions get cut out of the film, so your answer needs to make sense on its own.

If I ask "When did you start the business?" and you say "2011", that's no use to anyone watching. If you say "I started the business in 2011, from my kitchen table", that works. I'll remind you on the day, and if you forget, I'll just ask again.

You can stop and start again

Lost your thread halfway through? Stop, take a breath and start the sentence again. Said the wrong word? Say it again.

Nobody sees any of that. We edit. The ums, the long pauses, the false starts, the bit where you forgot what the question was. They all come out. What's left is you at your clearest, because we've got plenty of material to choose from.

What should I wear to be filmed?

Short version: wear what you'd normally wear for work, in its tidiest form. If you wear an apron behind the counter or overalls on site, wear them. The film is about your business, and you in a suit you never wear will look like someone else.

Fine stripes and tight checks do a thing on camera called moiré. Your shirt starts shimmering like it’s trying to hypnotise the viewer. Solid colours, every time.

A few things do matter on camera, though.

  • Solid, mid tones film best. Navy, mid grey, olive, a muted blue or green, earthy colours. They sit nicely on camera and suit most skin tones.
  • Avoid fine stripes, small checks and tight patterns. They can shimmer and flicker on camera, an effect called moiré. It's distracting, and it's very hard to fix later.
  • Avoid big logos and slogans. Especially other brands' logos. Your own company's branding is usually fine, but check with us first.
  • Be careful with bright white and solid black. They're harder to expose well next to a face. Not banned, just not the first choice.
  • Skip noisy jewellery. Bracelets and long necklaces knock against the microphone, and you'll hear it.

How does the microphone work?

For the interview you'll wear a small microphone, usually clipped to your collar or tucked just under your top, with a cable running to a little transmitter pack on your belt or waistband. Clothes with a collar or a proper waistband make this easier.

We'll show you where the cable needs to go and you can thread it through yourself. Nobody's going to be rummaging around your clothes without asking.

Two small things. Rustly fabrics like silk or stiff waterproofs can rub against the mic, so avoid them for the interview. And the mic is live until we take it off you, so if you nip to the loo, tell us first.

Most people forget they're wearing it within five minutes.

Should I tidy up before the crew arrives?

People worry a lot about how their space looks. My advice is to tidy the clutter that's just clutter, and leave everything that's the work.

Take out the bins. Clear the coffee cups off the desks. Move the pile of boxes that's been in the corner since Christmas. Turn off or tidy any screens with customer details or anything private on them.

But don't repaint, don't hide your tools and don't make a workshop look like a showroom. Real places look real on camera, and that's a big part of why people believe a documentary film. A bit of wear on the bench tells a viewer you actually use it.

What happens on the filming day?

Every shoot is different, but most days follow a similar shape.

  1. We arrive and have a look around. A coffee, a walk through the space, a chat about the day. No cameras rolling.
  2. We set up for the interview. Lights, sound and framing take a while to get right. You don't need to sit there while we do it.
  3. The interview. You sit down, get mic'd up and we talk. Expect it to take a lot longer than the bit that ends up on screen. That's normal.
  4. Filming you at work. This is the B-roll, the footage that plays while your voice carries on underneath. More on that below.
  5. Photography. Stills are captured across the same days, so you might find a camera pointing at you at odd moments.

What happens when you film me working?

The B-roll is you doing your job. Serving a customer, making something, fixing something, talking a colleague through something. The best advice I can give is to do it exactly the way you normally would, at your normal pace.

Don't look at the camera. Pretend we're not there, which gets easier after the first twenty minutes.

We might ask you to do something again. Maybe from a different angle, maybe because someone walked through the shot. That isn't because you did it wrong. A film needs the same moment from a few angles so it can be cut together smoothly. It can feel a bit repetitive. Bear with us.

How long does filming take?

A full film is usually two to three shoot days, but most people in it are only needed for part of that. Your bit might be a morning in the interview chair and a couple of hours of us following you around.

The whole project, from the first conversation to the finished film, usually takes six to ten weeks. Most of that is research before the shoot and the edit after it. You'll see a rough cut while changes are still easy to make, and again before it's finished, so nothing goes out that you haven't seen.

How do I deal with nerves on camera?

Everyone's nervous. Founders who pitch to investors get nervous. People who talk to customers all day get nervous. It's a camera and a stranger asking questions, so of course you are.

A few things genuinely help:

  • Talk to me, not the camera. You're having a conversation with a person who's interested in what you do.
  • Eat something beforehand and keep some water nearby.
  • Remember the first few minutes are a warm-up. People loosen up as they go, and the best answers usually come later.
  • Remember you're the expert in the room. Nobody knows your business better than you do, and that's all you're being asked about.

A bit of nerves on camera is no bad thing either. It usually reads as caring about what you do, which is exactly what we're trying to show. Frankly, I'd rather film someone who's a bit nervous and means every word than someone who's polished and says nothing. The first one makes a better film every time.

If you've got questions before the day, or you want to see what the finished films actually look like, have a look at our films or get in touch. We'd much rather answer a worry a week before the shoot than find out about it on the morning.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Will I get the interview questions in advance?
faqs.a: You'll know roughly what we'll talk about, but it's better not to have exact questions to rehearse. People who memorise their answers sound like they're reading, even when they're not. Think about a few stories instead: how you started, a day that went wrong, a customer you remember, the part of the job you're proudest of. If it'd put your mind at rest, ask and we'll talk you through the areas beforehand.

faqs.q: Should I wear make-up for a filmed interview?
faqs.a: You don't need to. Lights can make skin look shiny, so a little translucent powder or a matte moisturiser on the forehead and nose helps, for men as much as women. If you normally wear make-up, wear what you'd put on for an ordinary working day. Heavy make-up done specially for the camera tends to make you look like someone else, and the film's meant to look like you.

faqs.q: Can I see the film before it's published?
faqs.a: Yes. You'll see a rough cut while changes are still cheap and easy to make, and again before it's finished, so nothing goes out that you haven't seen. If an answer came out wrong, or there's something you'd rather wasn't in it, the rough cut is the time to say so. Changing the structure then is far easier than changing it after the grade and sound mix are done.

faqs.q: What if I really don't want to be on camera?
faqs.a: Tell us early, because there's usually a way round it. Not everyone in a business has to be interviewed, and a film can lean on whoever's happiest talking, whether that's a colleague or a customer. You could appear only in the shots of the work, with no interview at all. A bit of nerves is completely normal, though, and most people are fine once the conversation gets going.

items.title: Why good tripods cost so much
items.excerpt: Why good video tripods cost more: fluid heads vs ball heads, why smooth pans matter, what makes legs stable, counterbalance and what each budget buys you.
items.coverAlt: Two people at a table in a field above a fjord, a steady wide shot from a documentary
items.body:
Good video tripods cost more mainly because of the head. A fluid head uses thick grease inside to dampen movement, so a pan starts and stops smoothly instead of sticking and then lurching, and the legs underneath are stiff enough not to flex or twist. Cheap tripods usually cut corners on both. For stills that barely matters. For video, where the camera moves while it's recording, it's most of the job.

It's also why a tripod is one of the few bits of kit that doesn't really age. A camera from ten years ago looks dated. A good fluid head from ten years ago still does exactly what it did on day one, which tells you where the money went.

What's the difference between a fluid head and a ball head?

A ball head is built for photography. It's a ball in a socket that you loosen, point the camera wherever you want, then lock tight. It's quick, light and great for stills, because the camera doesn't need to move during the shot. Try to pan with one and it either won't move or it flops, because it's designed to be either locked or loose.

A fluid head is built for moving the camera while recording. Inside, sealed chambers of thick fluid or grease resist the movement, a bit like stirring honey. That resistance, called drag, means the camera moves at the speed your hand moves, without jumps. You can usually set how much drag you want for pan and tilt separately: more for slow, controlled moves on a long lens, less for quick reframing.

In between sit friction heads, which you'll find on a lot of cheaper "video" tripods. They use plain friction instead of fluid. They're fine for locking off a static shot. On a pan, they tend to grip, then slip, and the shot jerks at the start and end of every move.

Why do smooth pans matter so much?

Because the viewer's eye goes straight to anything that moves when it shouldn't. A pan that hesitates, jerks or bounces at the end pulls attention away from whatever you were showing and onto the camera. Once someone's noticed the camera, they've stepped out of the film for a second.

Smooth movement is also about control. The start and end of a move are the hardest parts, and a fluid head lets you ease in and ease out, which is what makes a pan feel deliberate rather than accidental. Even when the camera's not moving, a solid head and legs mean a locked-off shot stays perfectly still, which matters more than you'd think on a long interview or a close-up where tiny shakes get magnified.

A cheap tripod is a very reliable way of turning a slow, elegant pan into a short film about an earthquake.

What makes a tripod stable?

Stability is mostly about the legs. A few things make the difference:

  • Stiffness. Good legs resist twisting as well as bending. When you pan, the head pushes against the legs, and flimsy ones wind up and spring back, which shows as a little wobble at the end of the move.
  • Fewer, thicker sections. Every extra joint in a leg is a place for flex. Legs that fold down very small often pay for it in stiffness.
  • Spreaders. A brace that links the legs, either near the ground or halfway up, stops them sliding apart and adds rigidity.
  • No tall centre column. Photo tripods often have a column that winds up the middle. Raised high, it turns a stable tripod into a camera on a stick.
  • A levelling bowl. Video tripods often have a bowl at the top that the head sits in, so you can level the head in seconds without fiddling with each leg. That matters, because a head that isn't level will tilt the horizon as you pan.
  • Material. Carbon fibre is lighter and damps vibration well. Aluminium is heavier and cheaper. Both can be excellent. Weight matters more if you're carrying it all day.

What is counterbalance, and do you need it?

Counterbalance is a spring inside better fluid heads that pushes back against the weight of the camera as you tilt it. With it set correctly, you can tilt the camera up or down, let go, and it stays exactly where you left it. Without it, a heavy camera tilted forward wants to keep going, and you're fighting gravity on every move.

The setting needs to match the weight on top. Every head has a payload range, and it matters at both ends. Too heavy and it can't hold the camera. Too light and the spring pushes the camera back up. When you're working out what to buy, add up the camera, lens, microphone, monitor and anything else you'll mount, and pick a head whose range sits comfortably around that number.

The best camera support is the one nobody watching ever thinks about.

Our film about Signwriting Jack is built on close, patient coverage of the hand work, filmed at the speed it actually happens. That kind of shot lives or dies on the frame staying calm while the hand moves. Any wobble in the picture and your eye goes to the wobble instead of the brush.

What should you look for at different budgets?

I won't name products here, because models change every year and the categories matter more. Roughly, tripods fall into four groups.

  • Photo tripods with a ball head. Fine for static shots and interviews where the camera never moves. Not built for pans.
  • Budget "video" tripods. Usually a friction head and thin legs. They'll hold a phone or a light camera still. Expect sticky pans and some wobble.
  • Entry-level fluid heads on proper video legs. The point where it starts to feel right. Real fluid drag, a levelling bowl, usually a fixed counterbalance, and legs stiff enough for a small camera. For most people filming their own content, this is where I'd spend.
  • Professional systems. Heads with several steps of drag and adjustable counterbalance, larger bowls, twin-tube legs and spreaders. Built for heavier cinema cameras and long days, and built to last for many years.

Because good heads last so long, the second-hand market is worth a look, and hiring for a shoot day is a sensible option if you only need one now and then. What I wouldn't do is spend heavily on a camera and then put it on the cheapest legs going. The tripod is what decides whether the shot holds still.

Do you always need a tripod?

Not always. Handheld camera work has its own feel, closer and more alive, and it suits some moments in a documentary well. Gimbals and other stabilisers do smooth walking shots that a tripod can't. But for interviews, for slow detail shots and for anything where the camera needs to sit quietly and watch, the tripod is still the tool. If you're commissioning a film, this is part of what the day rate covers, and it's one reason a quote for a proper crew looks different to a quote for one person with a camera. There's more on where that money goes in how much a brand film costs in the UK, and on how camera movement shapes the feel of a film in what cinematography actually means.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a photography tripod for video?
faqs.a: For shots where the camera doesn't move, yes. A photo tripod with a ball head will hold a camera still for an interview or a locked-off wide. It won't give you smooth pans or tilts, though, because ball heads are designed to be either locked or loose. If you plan to move the camera during a shot, you need a fluid head.

faqs.q: Is carbon fibre worth it for a tripod?
faqs.a: It's worth it if you carry the tripod a lot. Carbon fibre legs are noticeably lighter than aluminium and absorb vibration well, which helps on long days and location shoots. Aluminium is cheaper, heavier and perfectly stable when well made. If the tripod mostly lives in a studio or the boot of a car, good aluminium legs are a sensible saving.

faqs.q: What does a 75mm or 100mm bowl mean on a tripod?
faqs.a: It's the size of the levelling bowl at the top of video tripod legs, where the head sits. The bowl lets you level the head quickly without adjusting each leg. Smaller bowls usually suit lighter camera setups, and larger bowls are built for heavier cameras and bigger heads. The head and legs need matching bowl sizes, or an adapter.

faqs.q: How long does a good tripod last?
faqs.a: Many years, often well over a decade with basic care. Good fluid heads and legs are built to be serviced rather than replaced, which is why they hold their value and why the second-hand market is busy. Keep the leg locks clean, avoid sand and salt water where you can, and have the head serviced if the drag ever starts to feel uneven.

items.title: What a brand film shoot day in London actually looks like
items.excerpt: From the recce and permits to the interview, the B-roll and the edit: how a documentary brand film shoot day in London really runs, start to finish.
items.coverAlt: A handmade earring being worn, filmed in the shop
items.body:
A shoot day for a documentary brand film in London is usually one long, full day: an early setup, a long interview, then the work filmed as it actually happens, with stills taken alongside. Most of what makes it go well is settled weeks before, in the research, the recce and the permits.

I'll be honest, the day itself is the easy bit. Most people who ask us about a film have never been on a shoot, so here's how one really runs for us, start to finish.

What happens before a brand film shoot day?

By the time a camera comes out, we should already know what the film is about. That comes from research and pre-interviews: time with the people who'll be in it, finding out what they've been through and what nobody outside the business knows. We come back with the story we think it is, and the client tells us whether we've got it right.

Then there's the recce. I want to stand in the space before the shoot, ideally at the time of day we'll be filming. I'm looking at where the light falls at ten in the morning, whether there's a fridge humming in the corner, whether the window behind the obvious interview chair will blow out on camera, and where we can put the kit so it's out of everyone's way. Twenty minutes on a recce saves an hour on the day.

Out of that comes a plan. Who we're interviewing and in what order, the work we need to see happen, where the interview goes, and a rough schedule that leaves room for things to run over. It will change on the day. That's normal.

Do you need a permit to film in London?

Sometimes, yes. If any of the day happens in a public space, the pavement outside, a park, a market, you may well need permission first. Each borough has its own process for filming on its streets, and the Royal Parks and Transport for London run their own. A small crew with handheld kit is often treated more lightly than a full unit with lights, cables and a generator, but the rules vary from place to place, so we check rather than assume.

Every London borough handles filming slightly differently. Nobody quite knows why. Plan for it anyway.

Then there's getting there. Parking near most London locations runs from difficult to impossible, and a car full of cases on a single yellow line is a bad start to anyone's morning. Depending on the location we'll sort a loading bay, a parking suspension if the shoot genuinely needs a vehicle outside, or just travel lighter. The Congestion Charge and ULEZ go into the plan as well, because they affect the call time as much as the cost.

What happens when the crew arrives?

Call time is usually early. The first hour goes on setup, and nobody being filmed needs to watch that happen.

We build the interview first, because it's the spine of the film and the part with the least room for error. The light gets shaped so the room looks like itself on a good day, rather than a studio someone dropped into the corner. Sound gets more attention than picture: a lav mic and a second mic overhead, levels checked, and then we go round switching off whatever we can. Fridges, air con, the radio in the back. And somebody writes a note to switch the fridge back on before we leave.

On a working site, all of this has to fit around the business. We filmed La Fromagerie during trading hours, around customers, including in cheese rooms that are cold, dark and full of people. Nothing stopped for us and nothing should have.

How is the interview filmed?

The interview is a conversation. Nothing read off an autocue, no script handed over the night before. I'll have questions, but the good material nearly always comes from following up on something the person said in passing.

It runs long, often well over an hour. People spend the first stretch giving the answers they think they're supposed to give. Somewhere past that they relax, and they start telling you what actually happened. I ask them to answer in full sentences, folding the question into the answer, because my voice won't be in the finished film and the answer has to make sense on its own.

Some films need a different setup. Deborah Carre and James Ducker of Carreducker are two founders who finish each other's sentences, so we filmed them together as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts, rather than as two separate interviews cut together afterwards.

How do you film the work itself?

After the interview, or sometimes around it, we film the work itself. As it happens, at the speed it happens. For Carreducker that meant close, patient coverage of the hand sewing and the bench work. Every pair goes through 210 steps and takes six months, and the parts that matter most are the slowest to watch, so you have to wait for them.

The interview usually tells you what to shoot next. If someone mentions a tool, a habit, a corner of the workshop, it goes on the list. That's how the pictures end up matching the words in the edit, instead of being generic shots laid over the top.

Some places fight you. Catherine Marche works at the bench and sells from a glass fronted shop, and reflections and mixed lighting fight you the whole way. You deal with it angle by angle. We shoot stills across the same day too, so the film and the photographs look like the same company.

Why use a small crew in London?

We keep crews small on purpose. Most of the places worth filming in London are tight: workshops, back rooms, shop floors, kitchens. A small crew fits, moves quickly, and doesn't block the pavement. It also changes how people behave. Someone being interviewed relaxes a lot faster with two people in the room than with eight, and for documentary that relaxation is the whole thing you're after.

In London, the smallest crew in the room is usually the one that gets the shot.

Then there's the city itself. Sirens, aircraft on the approach, building work starting up next door at the worst possible moment. You stop, wait, and go again. The light through the windows changes across the day too, so the schedule puts the interview where the light holds steadiest and moves the B-roll around it.

What if the work's already finished?

Not every shoot day catches the work in progress. Our renovation films for Nimrod Road in Tooting and Barry Road in East Dulwich were both filmed after the job was finished, with the families already moved back in. At Nimrod Road the before only exists in the original listing photos, so those got cut against the finished rooms. We filmed the street and the neighbourhood as well, because part of that couple's story is why they bought there in the first place.

That kind of shoot day is quieter. The interview carries far more of the weight, and the B-roll is about the finished spaces and the life going on in them.

What happens after the shoot day?

The edit starts with the interviews, not the pictures. Everything gets transcribed and the structure gets built on paper first, then pace, then picture. The client sees a rough cut while changing it is still cheap, and again before it's finished. After that the colour grade and the sound mix go to people who do only that.

Then come the cut-downs. Our main films usually run four to ten minutes, with a sixty to ninety second version for the top of a website and six to ten vertical pieces cut for the feed. For char.gy, one shoot turned into eleven finished exports: the long film, a sixty second cut and a thirty second cut, each in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1, plus an audio described version of the long film and the sixty second cut.

From first conversation to finished film is usually six to ten weeks, and most of that is the bit you can't rush. If you want to see what comes out the other end, the films page has the process and the work side by side.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How many people are in a brand film crew?
faqs.a: For a documentary brand film it's usually a small crew: one camera, proper sound and only the people the day actually needs. We keep it small on purpose. London workshops, shop floors and kitchens are tight, a small crew moves quickly, and people being interviewed relax much faster with two people in the room than with eight. Every extra person adds a day rate without always adding anything to the film.

faqs.q: Do we have to close the business on filming day?
faqs.a: No, and we'd usually rather you didn't. A shop filmed after hours looks empty and a bit lifeless, and the point of a documentary is showing the business as it really runs. La Fromagerie stayed open and trading the whole time we filmed. We work around customers and staff, and only ask for small things, like switching off a noisy fridge during the interview and switching it back on afterwards.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book a brand film?
faqs.a: Allow six to ten weeks from the first conversation to the finished film, and longer if it has to land on a fixed date like a launch or an event. Most of that time goes on research before the shoot and the edit after it. If you need something next week, a documentary film is the wrong purchase. Get in touch early and work back from the date you actually need it.

faqs.q: Does a film crew need insurance to shoot on my premises?
faqs.a: Yes. Any professional crew should carry public liability insurance, and it's fair to ask for a copy of the certificate before the shoot. Plenty of landlords, venues and managed buildings won't let a crew in without it. Insuring the kit is the crew's own job, so that shouldn't land on you. If any filming happens in public space in London, the borough or landowner may also want to see cover before granting permission.
