items.title: Lav mics explained: microphones for interviews
items.excerpt: Lavalier, shotgun or handheld? How interview microphones differ, where a lav mic goes, how to hide it under clothing and how to fix rustle and wind noise.
items.coverAlt: Clipping a lav mic onto an interviewee before filming
items.body:
Most interviews are recorded on a lavalier mic, the small clip-on one, often with a shotgun mic on a boom pole above the speaker as well. The lav sits on the chest a few inches from the mouth, so it hears the voice clearly even in a noisy room. A boom sounds more natural but needs someone holding it, and a handheld mic is for news, events and vox pops, where nobody minds it being in the shot.

If you're paying for a film, sound is the part you'll notice least when it's right and most when it's wrong. People will sit through a slightly soft shot. They'll click away from a voice that crackles, booms or disappears under traffic.

What types of microphone are used for interviews?

Lavalier mics

A lav is a tiny microphone, about the size of a pea or smaller, on a thin cable that runs to a transmitter pack or a recorder on the belt. Being that close to the mouth means the voice is far louder than the room around it. Most lavs are omnidirectional, so they hear in every direction equally, and the speaker can turn their head without the level dropping away.

The catch is that a lav lives on clothing, so it hears clothing. Every brush of a lapel or tap on the chest goes straight into it.

Shotgun mics on a boom

A shotgun is a long, narrow microphone that mostly hears what it's pointed at and turns down sound from the sides. On an interview it's held on a boom pole just above the top of the frame, angled down at the mouth, by a sound recordist who follows the speaker. Because it sits in the air rather than on the body, it sounds open and natural, closer to how you'd hear the person if you were sat across the table from them.

It needs a reasonably quiet room and someone whose whole job is holding it, and in a small room with hard walls it picks up more echo.

Handheld mics

The one you see on the news. It's tough and good at ignoring background noise, and it's in the shot, which is fine for an event or a reporter stopping people in the street. For a documentary it's usually wrong, because it turns a conversation into a press interview and everyone watching can feel it.

Why use a lav and a boom together?

On a properly crewed interview you'll often see both running at once, recorded to separate tracks. The boom gives the more natural sound, and the lav covers the moments when a bus goes past or the speaker leans out of the boom's sweet spot. Two microphones on one voice is cheap insurance on a recording you can't get back.

If you're filming on your own, a lav on its own is usually the better bet. A shotgun sat on top of the camera is too far from the speaker for a sit-down interview and hears the room as much as the voice.

Where should a lav mic go?

The usual spot is the middle of the chest, on the breastbone, roughly a hand's width below the chin. That's close enough for a strong, clear voice and far enough down that breaths and lip noise don't take over. Go higher, onto a collar, and the voice gets thinner and changes every time the person looks down. Go lower, towards the stomach, and the room starts creeping in.

Two things decide the exact spot:

  • Which way they'll turn. If the interviewer sits to the speaker's left, put the mic a touch left of centre so the voice stays on it when they turn to answer.
  • Jewellery, lanyards and ties. Anything that can swing will tap the mic. Take it off or tape it down.

Visible or hidden is a choice. A small mic clipped neatly to a shirt is completely normal in a documentary, and it usually sounds better than a hidden one. When someone's in their own clothes in their own workshop, I'd rather see a tidy mic than lose half a sentence to rustle.

How do you hide a lav mic under clothing?

Hiding a lav is a small craft of its own, and the aim is always the same. Stop the mic moving against the fabric, and stop the fabric moving against the mic.

  • Tape it down. Sound recordists use double-sided toupee tape, often folded around the mic so there's a layer between the capsule and the cloth, then fixed to the skin or the inside of the shirt.
  • Build a small gap. A soft pad or a purpose-made cover between the mic and the shirt stops the two rubbing directly.
  • Loop the cable. A small loop taped just below the mic soaks up any tug, so a movement at the belt doesn't drag the capsule across the fabric.
  • Keep the front clear. The mic needs to face out through as few layers as possible. Under a thin cotton shirt is fine. Under a heavy jumper the voice goes muffled.

Clothing matters more than people expect. Cotton and wool are quiet. Synthetics, waterproofs, silk and stiff new shirts crackle every time someone breathes. If you're the one being filmed, plain cotton is the easy answer, and there's more on that in how to prepare for being filmed.

Nothing tests a working relationship like asking a managing director if you can tape something to their chest. Ask first, explain why, and offer to let them do it themselves.

Why does my lav mic sound scratchy?

Nearly always it's clothing rustle. It sounds like crackling, scratching or a dull thump, and it lines up with the speaker moving their arms, shifting in the chair or patting their chest to make a point. It's one of the hardest things to clean up afterwards, because the noise sits right on top of the voice.

Before you blame the mic, check these:

  • Is the clip or tape loose, so the mic can slide?
  • Is the cable rubbing on a seam or a button further down?
  • Is a necklace, lanyard or tie touching it?
  • Is the person a hand talker? Some people tap their chest on every point. Move the mic slightly off centre, away from that hand.

If the voice crunches when someone laughs, that's a different problem: the level's set too high and the recording is clipping. Noise reduction in the edit can soften rustle, though push it too far and the voice sounds watery. Fixing it on the day is always better, which is the whole argument for a second mic.

People will sit through a slightly soft shot. They'll click away from a voice that crackles.

How do you stop wind noise on a lav?

Outside, the enemy is wind. Even a light breeze across an uncovered mic causes a low rumble and loud pops that wreck a sentence. The fix is a windshield: a small foam cover for gentle air, and a furry cover, which the industry calls a dead cat, for anything stronger. The fur slows the air down before it reaches the capsule.

A hidden lav has a head start, because the clothing works as a windshield. It's one of the few times hiding the mic actually helps. Beyond that, the easy wins are turning the speaker's back to the wind, using a wall or a doorway as shelter, and recording thirty seconds of the location on its own, called room tone or a wild track, so the editor has something to smooth the gaps with.

If you've ever seen what looks like a small grey animal on a pole at a film shoot, that's a boom in its windshield.

Our film for Carreducker is a good example of why interview sound needs planning. Two founders who finish each other's sentences, filmed as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts. Two voices overlapping in a workshop is a sound problem as much as a picture one, because each person has to come through clearly for the edit to hold together.

What does this mean if you're paying for a film?

Ask who's looking after sound on the day. On a small shoot it might be the camera operator doing both, which can work for one interview in a quiet room. For more than one voice, a noisy location or someone moving about, a dedicated sound recordist earns their day rate quickly. It's worth asking who does the sound mix too. On our films the grade and mix are done by people who only do that, and the films page shows how the rest fits together. If the mic is wireless, there's a second set of things that can go wrong, which I've covered in how wireless audio works for interviews.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a phone with a lav mic for interviews?
faqs.a: Yes, and for someone filming on their own it's one of the cheapest big improvements you can make. A wired lav plugged into a phone puts the mic close to the mouth, which matters far more than the recording device. Check the connector suits your phone, keep the cable out of shot, and do a short test recording with headphones before you start the real interview.

faqs.q: Should a lav mic be visible on camera?
faqs.a: It can be, and in documentary and interview work it usually is. A small mic clipped neatly to the centre of a shirt looks normal to viewers and generally sounds better than a hidden one. Hiding it makes sense for drama, for scenes where the person moves around a lot, or when a visible mic would clash with the look the client wants.

faqs.q: What clothes cause the most microphone noise?
faqs.a: Synthetic fabrics, waterproof jackets, silk, stiff new shirts and anything with a zip or loose buttons near the chest. They crackle and rub against the mic every time the person moves or breathes. Soft cotton and wool are the quietest. Avoid noisy jewellery and lanyards too, because anything that swings will tap the microphone during the interview.

faqs.q: How many microphones does an interview need?
faqs.a: One good microphone close to the speaker is the minimum, and a lav does that job well. A professional crew will often add a boom mic on a second track as a backup and for a more natural sound. With two people talking, each person needs their own mic so the editor can control each voice separately.

items.title: How to make a brand video people actually watch
items.excerpt: A person with something at stake, an interview as the spine, and the nerve to cut what's merely nice. What keeps people watching a brand film to the end.
items.coverAlt: Hand painted signwriting, filmed in the workshop and on the street
items.body:
People watch a brand video to the end when there's a real person in it with something at stake, when it starts where something's already happening, and when whoever edited it had the nerve to cut everything that wasn't needed. It also has to be made for a reason. A lovely film with no job to do gets watched once, mostly by the people who paid for it.

Most brand videos get signed off by people who already care about the company. Everyone in that meeting knows the product, likes the logo and wants it to do well, so the video passes. Then it goes on the website and a stranger gives it a few seconds before they're gone.

The films people finish are made with that stranger in mind from the very first conversation. This is what I think actually makes the difference, from the films we've made and the plenty I've switched off myself.

Who should a brand video be about?

People watch people. Someone telling you about a decision that could have gone badly is a lot harder to leave.

Stakes don't have to be dramatic. In our film about a period house in Tooting, the couple bought a Victorian house that had sat empty since the previous owners died. The renovation started in September and they had a baby due at the end of November. That's all the tension the film needs. You want to know whether they made it, and you keep watching to find out.

Every business has something like that if you look properly. A founder who nearly gave up. A craft that took years to learn. A customer who took a risk on you. The work is finding it before anyone turns up with a camera.

What's the film actually for?

I'll say this plainly, because it's the thing people skip. Filming alone often isn't enough. A great film with nothing planned around it gets a launch post, a few kind comments from people who already know you, and then it sits on the About page.

Filming on its own isn’t enough. A film earns its money when it’s built for a job.

The work lands when the creative is tied to the goal or the campaign it's there to serve. That decision shapes everything: who's in it, how it opens, how long it runs and which cuts come out of it. The Barry Road film was made to be an edit a builder can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. The char.gy film runs as the principal video on two pages of their site. Both had a job before a frame was shot.

So before you talk about cameras or locations, be clear about where the film's going to live and what you want someone to do after watching it. If you can't answer that, you're not ready to shoot yet.

Should you plan the story before filming?

Yes, and properly. Most of what decides whether a film works happens before the shoot. Research, pre-interviews, time spent working out which story is actually the one. The obvious story is usually the product. The one people watch is usually the person behind it, or the part of the process nobody outside ever sees.

How should a brand video start?

In the middle. Don't open with the logo, the company history or someone saying their name and job title. Start where something is already happening. A line from the interview that makes you lean in, or the work half done.

The context can come later. Viewers are surprisingly happy to catch up as long as they've got a reason to. What they won't sit through is a slow warm up before anything interesting has happened.

Should a brand video have a voiceover?

I'd almost always say no. For documentary brand films, the interview carries the story and the pictures follow it. Get the interview right and the edit has something to hang off. Get it wrong and no amount of B-roll will fix it.

That means a real conversation with nothing read off an autocue, and enough time that the person stops performing. In my experience the best line often turns up late, once they've forgotten the camera.

It also means skipping the voice of god. A narrator telling you how good a company is carries no weight, because you know someone paid for those words. When a London builder wanted a film about a full house renovation, we handed it to the homeowner. The only version a prospective client believes is the one from someone who has already handed over the money.

Should you cut fast to keep people watching?

Mostly no. The instinct in an edit is to cut fast so nobody gets bored. Usually it does the opposite. When someone pauses before an answer, or a hand does something difficult, holding on it is what makes people watch.

With Signwriting Jack, the value is the single unbroken line that either works or doesn't. Cut away halfway through and you've thrown out the one moment that proves the skill. Craft films in particular need the patience to show the work at the speed it's actually done.

How much does sound matter?

More than most people think. Viewers will forgive slightly soft footage. They won't sit through bad audio. A clean interview recording is the minimum, and after that, real sound from the place does a lot of quiet work: the brush on the board, the needle through leather, the noise of a shop that's open and trading.

On a drainage job we filmed for Super Efficient, some of the vertical cuts left the jetter and the water alone rather than burying them under music. That sound is the satisfying bit. Covering it would have made the clip worse.

How much music should a brand video have?

Less than you'd expect. Music is the easiest way to make a film feel like an advert. Wall to wall, swelling at all the expected points, it tells the viewer how to feel, and most people can sense that and pull back a little.

If the music’s doing all the emotional work, the film isn’t.

Use it where it earns a place. Under a transition, to lift a moment that's already working, to give the ending some space. Then let it drop out when someone's saying something that matters. Silence in the right place lands harder than any track.

What should you cut?

Anything that's merely nice. This is the hardest part of any edit. You'll have shots you love, a drone pass that cost a morning, an answer that's lovely but goes nowhere. If it doesn't move the story on, it comes out.

I ask the same thing of every scene: would anyone miss it? If the honest answer is no, it goes, however good it looks. A shorter film that holds attention all the way through beats a longer one that loses people at the halfway mark.

How long should a brand video be?

There's no correct length for a brand film. There's only the length the story can carry. Our main films usually run four to ten minutes, because that's the room some stories need, but every one comes with a sixty to ninety second cut for the places where nobody's going to give you ten minutes, and vertical pieces cut for the feed.

What doesn't work is a two minute story stretched to six because someone thought longer looked more premium. People feel the padding and they leave.

What does that look like in a real film?

When char.gy were certified as a B Corp, they had a problem. Certification is a genuinely hard thing to earn and a genuinely dull thing to explain. The easy version puts a score on screen and hopes people are impressed.

We did it the other way round. The char.gy film lets the people who did the work explain why it mattered, from the team who ran the certification to the engineers on the street. It was cut into a long version, a sixty second and a thirty second cut, with an audio described version so people who can't see it can still follow it. It's now the most viewed video on their YouTube channel.

More of our work is on the films page, and if you've got a story you think is worth telling, that's where to start.

faqs.q: Should brand videos have subtitles?
faqs.a: Yes, especially anything going on social. Plenty of people scroll with the sound off, so vertical cuts need captions to make sense at all. On the main film, subtitles help anyone watching somewhere they can't play sound, and they're an accessibility basic for viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing. Go further where it fits, like the audio described version we made for char.gy, so people who can't see the screen can follow it too.

faqs.q: Is one long brand film better than lots of short videos?
faqs.a: You don't have to choose if the shoot's planned properly. One shoot can give you the main film, usually four to ten minutes, a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of your site and six to ten vertical pieces for the feed. The long film earns trust with people who are already interested. The short cuts reach the people who'd never give you ten minutes in the first place.

faqs.q: How do you measure whether a brand video worked?
faqs.a: Measure it against the job you gave it before filming. If it was made to help sales, look at whether buyers who watched it move faster or stall less. If it was for hiring, look at the quality of applications. For views, check how far people get as well as how many start, because a film people finish is doing its work. YouTube and social analytics show you retention for free.

faqs.q: Where should I share my brand video once it's finished?
faqs.a: Put it where people are deciding whether to trust you. That's usually your homepage or a key service page, YouTube, sales emails and proposals, recruitment pages and any events you run. The short cut goes at the top of the site, and the vertical pieces go out on social over the following weeks. A single launch post won't do much on its own, so plan where the film keeps working after that.

stat.title: How people most like to learn about a product or service
stat.takeaway: People choose a short video over everything else by a mile, so keep your film tight and make every second earn its place.
